search.t: 1 Chapter 1 Entrepreneurship: Concept and Importance Entrepreneurship is talked about so much in the media and in support programs that the term has come to be applied to every commercial activity. But the concept has a more precise scientific meaning, shaped by a century of research in economics and management. In this chapter we start by defining the concept and its schools of thought, then distinguish the entrepreneurial venture from others, present the types of entrepreneurship and their role in the economy, and end with the features of the entrepreneurial ecosystem in Saudi Arabia. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, you should be able to: Define entrepreneurship and distinguish it from traditional trade and small business management. Name the types of entrepreneurship and give an example of each. Explain the role of entrepreneurship in the Saudi economy and its support ecosystem.

search.c: Chapter 1: Entrepreneurship: Concept and Importance | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: The Arabic word for entrepreneurship, riyada , comes from al-ra'id : the scout who rides ahead of the tribe to find water and pasture before everyone moves. That old meaning brings us close to the modern concept. The scout goes where others have not gone, bears the hardship and uncertainty of exploring, and comes back with something that benefits the group. The English word comes from the French verb entreprendre , "to undertake" or "to take something on." Definitions of entrepreneurship vary in the scholarly literature because people look at it from different angles. Economists look at its effect on markets, management scholars at how resources are organized, and psychologists at the person who does it. Yet these definitions meet at one core, which we can put this way: Entrepreneurship is the process of discovering an opportunity to solve a problem or meet a need, and turning it, through innovation, into a venture that adds value for people, by organizing the resources required, while bearing a calculated degree of risk and uncertainty. Let us take this definition apart, because every word in it carries meaning: "Process" : entrepreneurship is not a single moment of inspiration. It is a series of steps that starts with observation, moves through testing and adjustment, and continues as the venture grows. That is why it can be learned step by step. "Discovering an opportunity" : the starting point is neither money nor a company. It is an opportunity: a problem that has not been solved well, a need that has not been met, or a change in society or technology that opens a new door. "Through innovation" : entrepreneurship does not repeat what already exists; it offers something new or a better way. Innovation here does not mean invention. It may be a new product, a service delivered in an easier way, a different business model, or a market that has not been served before. This is what sets an entrepreneurial venture apart, as we will see shortly. "Organizing resources" : the entrepreneur does not need to own every resource, but must know how to gather and organize them: money, people, knowledge, relationships and time. "Adds value" : an entrepreneurial venture makes someone's life better. It saves them time, money or effort, or offers something that was not available before. Without that value, nobody will pay. "Calculated risk and uncertainty" : entrepreneurs work in conditions where the outcome is not known in advance. But they do not gamble; they reduce risk through study and small experiments. Creativity, innovation and entrepreneurship: one chain. Creativity is generating a new and useful idea; innovation is turning it into a product, service or method that people actually use; entrepreneurship is building a venture around that innovation that can survive: gathering its resources, bearing its risk, and getting it to the people who need it and will pay for it. An idea alone does not make a venture, and a venture that offers nothing new remains a copy of what exists. We will look more closely at creativity and innovation in Chapter 4.

search.c: Chapter 1: Entrepreneurship: Concept and Importance | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: You do not need to memorize many theories, but knowing three main schools of thought helps explain why we talk about entrepreneurship the way we do. 1. The innovation school: Schumpeter The Austrian economist Joseph Schumpeter was among the first to place the entrepreneur at the heart of economic theory, in The Theory of Economic Development (1934 in its English translation). Schumpeter argued that economies do not develop through the accumulation of capital alone, but through people who bring "new combinations" to the market. He named five forms: a new product, a new method of production, a new market, a new source of raw materials, or a new organization of an industry. Schumpeter also coined a famous idea, creative destruction : every successful innovation pushes aside what came before it. When smartphones with good cameras spread, sales of compact digital cameras fell; when streaming services appeared, video and disc rentals declined. This destruction hurts the old firms, but it is "creative" because it moves the economy to a better level of service. 2. The practice school: Drucker Peter Drucker, one of the leading management thinkers of the twentieth century, moved entrepreneurship from a mysterious trait to a systematic practice . In Innovation and Entrepreneurship (1985) he describes the entrepreneur as someone who "always searches for change, responds to it, and exploits it as an opportunity." Drucker's most important contribution is that entrepreneurship is not limited to small new businesses: a hospital, a university or a government agency can be entrepreneurial if it manages innovation systematically. We will return in Chapter 3 to the seven sources of opportunity he identified. 3. The opportunity school: Shane and Venkataraman In 2000, Scott Shane and S. Venkataraman published an influential article proposing that the subject of entrepreneurship research is the opportunity : how it is discovered, evaluated and exploited, and by whom. The focus shifted from "Who is the entrepreneur?" to "How does a particular person meet a particular opportunity?" This view is useful for students, because it means entrepreneurship does not require an extraordinary personality. It requires an eye that notices opportunities and the ability to move toward them. The three schools in brief: the entrepreneur creates something new (Schumpeter), does so through a systematic practice that looks for change (Drucker), and all of this revolves around an opportunity that is discovered and pursued (Shane and Venkataraman).

search.c: Chapter 1: Entrepreneurship: Concept and Importance | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 1-3 The Entrepreneur, the Trader and the Small Business Owner
search.t: Many people confuse entrepreneurship with owning any business. In fact, the difference lies neither in the size of the venture nor in its type, but in two things: the degree of innovation (does the venture offer new value or a better way?) and the ambition to grow (does it seek to expand, or is it content with its size?). Dimension Traditional business Entrepreneurial venture Starting point A known model, proven in the market A problem or opportunity that is poorly served Innovation Low: repeats what exists Medium to high: offers something different Risk and uncertainty Lower, because the market and demand are known Higher, because the model itself needs proof Growth Linear and gradual Aims for fast, scalable growth Example A neighborhood grocery selling what other groceries sell A platform that connects neighborhood groceries with residents and delivers orders within an hour A real-world example makes this clearer. Someone opens a café serving the same coffee in the same way on a street that already has ten cafés. This is a legitimate and useful business, but it is not entrepreneurship in the precise sense. Someone else notices that staff at the nearby hospital work night shifts and cannot find good coffee after midnight, so they set up a pre-ordered coffee delivery service for night shifts. This is closer to entrepreneurship, because it starts from an unserved need and offers a different solution. This does not make traditional businesses less valuable. They are an essential part of the economy and provide many jobs. But this course focuses on the mindset that looks for new value, because that skill serves you in any field.

search.c: Chapter 1: Entrepreneurship: Concept and Importance | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: When we hear the word "entrepreneurship," we usually picture an app or a tech company. But entrepreneurship is much broader than that, and it can be classified by goal and by the nature of growth: 1. Small business entrepreneurship A venture set up by one person or a few partners as a stable source of income, serving a limited local community: a repair workshop, a home kitchen, a small training center. Its owner does not necessarily seek large-scale expansion, but stability and quality of service. It is entrepreneurial when it offers something different in its local market. 2. Scalable startups A venture searching for a business model that can be repeated and grown very fast, serving thousands or millions of customers without its costs multiplying at the same rate. Startups usually rely on technology, need outside investment, and accept high risk in exchange for the chance of a large return. Steve Blank defines a startup as "a temporary organization in search of a repeatable and scalable business model": it is in a phase of searching and testing, not of executing a known plan. 3. Social entrepreneurship A venture whose first goal is to solve a social or environmental problem, such as employing people with disabilities, reducing food waste or educating underserved groups. It differs from charity in that it seeks financial sustainability : it earns enough from its activity to cover its costs and keep going, rather than relying entirely on donations. Profit here is a means, not an end. 4. Intrapreneurship Entrepreneurship practiced from inside an existing organization, public or private. The intrapreneur notices a problem in the organization's work, proposes a new solution and leads it through to implementation: a nurse who proposes a system that reduces medication errors, a teacher who develops a way to follow up with struggling students, or a government employee who automates a paper-based procedure. This type is the closest to most students after graduation, which is why we say this course is for everyone. 5. Family entrepreneurship Ventures owned and run by a family and passed between generations. Many of the large companies in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf began as a small shop. The entrepreneurial challenge here is renewal: how does the new generation preserve what the previous one built and develop it to fit a changing market? 6. Digital entrepreneurship Ventures based entirely or mostly online: e-commerce stores, content creation, apps and remotely delivered services. Their advantage is a relatively low cost of starting and the ability to reach customers beyond the city limits. But competition is fierce, because entry is easy for everyone.

search.c: Chapter 1: Entrepreneurship: Concept and Importance | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 1-5 Why Economies and Societies Care About Entrepreneurship
search.t: Governments, universities and organizations care about entrepreneurship because it plays roles that large companies cannot play alone: Creating jobs : small and medium enterprises employ a large share of workers in most economies, and every successful venture creates jobs for people other than its founder. Innovation : many of the products and services we use today came from small companies that were bolder and more flexible than the large ones, and then grew. Economic diversification : entrepreneurship opens new sectors, such as tourism, entertainment, technology and the creative industries, instead of relying on a single resource. This is a central goal of Saudi Vision 2030. Competition and better service : new entrants push existing businesses to improve quality and lower prices, and consumers benefit. Local development : small ventures serve the needs of cities and villages and keep money circulating in the local community. Empowering individuals : entrepreneurship gives young people and women a chance to build their own income and future.

search.c: Chapter 1: Entrepreneurship: Concept and Importance | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Saudi Vision 2030 made small and medium enterprises a central pillar of economic transformation, with a stated target of raising their contribution to GDP from about 20% to 35%. To get there, an entrepreneurial ecosystem has taken shape over recent years: a network of organizations that complement one another in supporting a venture from idea to growth. Its main components include: Organization Its role in the ecosystem Small and Medium Enterprises General Authority (Monsha'at) The regulator and supporter of the sector: training and mentoring programs, incubators and accelerators, entrepreneur service centers, and initiatives that simplify procedures. Social Development Bank Finances startups and freelance work, with preparation programs before financing. Kafalah program Guarantees part of the financing that banks give small enterprises, lowering the bank's risk and making loans easier to obtain. Saudi Venture Capital Company and Jada Fund of Funds Invest in venture capital and private equity funds, which in turn finance startups. Incubators and accelerators Programs that host ventures in their early stages, offering mentoring, space and networks, and sometimes early funding. University entrepreneurship centers The nearest starting point for students: competitions, workshops, mentoring and links to the ecosystem. These organizations work as a chain. A student may start with an idea in a university competition, then join an incubator that helps build a prototype, then receive early funding from a government program or an investor, and then grow and attract larger investment. Program details and requirements change constantly. Always check the organizations' official websites before applying to any program.

search.t: 2 Chapter 2 The Entrepreneurial Mindset Why does one person manage to turn a simple idea into a venture, while another has a better idea and never starts? A large part of the answer lies in the way of thinking. In this chapter we look at the behaviors that distinguish entrepreneurs, present the theory of effectuation, which explains how expert entrepreneurs make decisions under uncertainty, and then correct a number of common myths. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, you should be able to: Describe the core entrepreneurial traits and behaviors. Explain the five principles of effectuation. Distinguish between common myths and facts about entrepreneurship.

search.c: Chapter 2: The Entrepreneurial Mindset | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: This question occupied researchers for decades. Early on, many studies tried to find a stable "entrepreneurial personality" that sets entrepreneurs apart, such as a love of risk or a high need for achievement. But the results were contradictory: there were successful entrepreneurs who were very cautious, and risk-lovers who never succeeded in any venture. Modern research therefore turned to what entrepreneurs do rather than who they are. The conclusion most researchers agree on today is that entrepreneurship is a set of behaviors, skills and ways of thinking that grow with learning and practice, like the skill of writing or leading. Some people may have a stronger inclination toward it, but everyone can develop it. This is the scientific case for teaching this course to all students.

search.c: Chapter 2: The Entrepreneurial Mindset | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Here are the behaviors that recur most among entrepreneurs, with their practical meaning, because words like initiative and resilience can sound vague unless we show how they appear in real life. 1. Initiative Initiative means moving before you are asked, and taking responsibility for turning an observation into action. Many people notice problems and complain about them, but few ask: "What can I do?" An employee who notices that visitors ask the same question every day, and prepares a simple guide and posts it at the entrance, has acted entrepreneurially, even without turning it into a venture. 2. Calculated risk-taking The popular image is of the entrepreneur as an "adventurer" leaping into the unknown. In reality, successful entrepreneurs try to reduce risk, not seek it. Calculated risk means three things: knowing what could go wrong, deciding what you can afford to lose, and testing the idea in small steps before a big commitment. The difference between a gambler and an entrepreneur is that the gambler puts everything on one bet, while the entrepreneur tests with a small part and learns. 3. Tolerating ambiguity At the start of any venture you do not know many of the answers: Will people buy? At what price? Who is the real competitor? Some people feel intense anxiety in this situation and postpone decisions until the picture becomes clear, but it only becomes clear through action. Tolerating ambiguity means taking a reasonable step with the information available, then adjusting as new information appears. 4. Persistence and resilience Every venture's journey is full of rejection: a customer who does not reply, an investor who declines, an experiment that fails. Persistence is continuing despite this, and resilience is the ability to get up after failure without turning it into a judgment on yourself. Balance matters here: persistence does not mean insisting on an idea the evidence has shown does not work, but holding on to the goal while staying flexible about the route. 5. Creativity and problem solving The entrepreneur sees a problem as a possible opportunity and looks for unconventional solutions. This does not require genius ideas; sometimes it is enough to combine two existing things in a new way, or to move a solution from one field to another. 6. Customer orientation Successful entrepreneurs are more preoccupied with the customer than with their idea. They listen more than they speak, ask why people behave as they do, and change their minds when they see new evidence. A common mistake is for a student to fall in love with their idea and hear only what confirms it. 7. Continuous learning Nobody starts a venture knowing everything about marketing, finance, technology and law. Entrepreneurs discover what they lack and learn it quickly, from a course, a book, an expert, or from the experience itself. 8. Building relationships Relationships are among a venture's most important resources: the partner who complements your skills, the mentor who advises you, the first customer who trusts you, the supplier who gives you good terms. Many opportunities come through someone you know, not through an advertisement.

search.c: Chapter 2: The Entrepreneurial Mindset | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 2-3 How Do Expert Entrepreneurs Think? Effectuation Theory
search.t: One of the most important scientific contributions to understanding the entrepreneurial mindset comes from Saras Sarasvathy, professor of entrepreneurship at the University of Virginia. Sarasvathy studied how expert entrepreneurs who had founded successful companies make decisions. She gave them a hypothetical problem of starting a venture, asked them to think aloud, and compared their approach with that of managers in large corporations. She found two different logics of thinking: Causation Effectuation Starts with a specific goal, then looks for the means to reach it Starts with the means available, then sees which goals they make possible Relies on predicting the future and studying the market Treats the future as unpredictable, and shapes it through action Focuses on expected return Focuses on the loss that can be afforded Sees surprises as deviations from the plan Sees surprises as possible opportunities Example: "I want to open an Italian restaurant, so let's find a location, funding and a chef." Example: "I cook well, and I know office owners who order lunch every day, so let's start delivering meals to them and see where it takes us." This does not mean causal logic is wrong. It suits situations where the market is known and the future is predictable. But at the start of new ventures, where uncertainty is high, experts lean toward effectual logic. Sarasvathy summed it up in five principles, which we explain one by one: Principle 1: Bird in Hand Start with what you have now, not with what you wish you had. Three questions help you take stock of your resources: Who am I? (my interests, values and personality), What do I know? (my field, experience and skills), and Whom do I know? (family, friends, professors and contacts). Many students say "I have nothing to start with," but when they answer these questions they discover resources they had overlooked. A clinical nutrition student who knows home cooks in her family could start a service offering healthy meals tailored to people with diabetes in her neighborhood. Principle 2: Affordable Loss Instead of asking "How much will I make?", a question that cannot be answered accurately at the beginning, ask: "What can I lose in this experiment without it hurting me?" The answer might be "SAR 500 and two weekends." Risk then turns from something frightening into something limited and known, and you can start now instead of waiting. Principle 3: Crazy Quilt A patchwork quilt is sewn from different pieces of fabric brought by different people. The idea is to build your venture through partnerships with those who commit to you early, rather than spending your time analyzing competitors. A partner here might be a classmate who is good at design, a shop that agrees to trial your service, or a customer who pays in advance. Every partner who joins adds new resources, and may change the venture's direction as well. Principle 4: Lemonade From the saying "When life gives you lemons, make lemonade." Surprises and obstacles are not always bad; they may point to a better opportunity. A team that started selling simple software for managing clinic appointments noticed that clinics kept asking about sending patients reminders before their appointments. They added a reminder service, and it became their most requested and most profitable service. Principle 5: Pilot in the Plane The future is not only something we wait for and predict; it is something we help create through our actions. A pilot does not wait for the plane to carry them to their destination; they fly it and correct its course constantly. A student who waits for "the right time" or "the perfect idea" may wait a long time, while someone who starts with a small step shapes their own circumstances.

search.c: Chapter 2: The Entrepreneurial Mindset | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Some misconceptions stop many students from even considering entrepreneurship. Here are the best known, with corrections: Myth Reality Entrepreneurs are born, not made Entrepreneurial skills are acquired through learning and experience, as explained at the start of this chapter. You need a lot of capital to start Many ventures started with modest resources and tested the idea before asking for any funding. Money usually comes after proving the idea works. The idea is everything Ideas are plentiful and often repeated. What makes the difference is execution, learning from the customer and continuous adjustment. I always tell my students: the idea is about 5% of success, and execution 95%; a good idea is a condition, but it is not everything. Entrepreneurs are thrill-seekers who love danger Successful entrepreneurs reduce risk through small experiments and affordable loss. Failure is the end of the road Failure is a source of learning, and many successful people tried ventures that did not work before the one that did. Entrepreneurship is only for tech and business students Opportunities exist in health, education, agriculture, tourism, the arts and services. The best ideas often come from people in a field who know its problems from the inside. You must leave your studies or job to start You can start with a small side project and expand it gradually once it proves itself.

search.c: Chapter 2: The Entrepreneurial Mindset | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Psychologist Carol Dweck at Stanford University studied how people deal with challenge and failure, and distinguished between two mindsets: Fixed mindset : sees intelligence and talent as fixed traits that do not change. A person with this mindset avoids challenges for fear of exposing weakness, and sees failure as proof that they are "not good enough." Growth mindset : sees abilities as growing through effort, learning and practice. A person with this mindset accepts challenges and sees failure as information about what they need to learn. The importance of this concept in entrepreneurship is clear. When a customer rejects your idea, the fixed mindset says: "My idea is a failure and I'm not cut out for this." The growth mindset says: "What does this rejection tell me about the customer? What should I change?" The good news is that mindset itself can change; simply being aware of the difference helps you shift toward a growth mindset.

search.c: Chapter 2: The Entrepreneurial Mindset | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Entrepreneurship is a set of behaviors and skills acquired through practice, not an innate trait reserved for a few. Key entrepreneurial behaviors include initiative, calculated risk-taking, tolerating ambiguity, persistence and customer orientation. Expert entrepreneurs start with the resources in hand, set an affordable loss, build partnerships and turn surprises into opportunities. A growth mindset turns rejection and failure into sources of learning.

search.t: 3 Chapter 3 Opportunities and Idea Generation Every venture starts with an idea, but not every idea is fit to become a venture. In this chapter we distinguish between ideas and opportunities, present the sources from which opportunities arise as Drucker classified them, and then offer practical techniques for generating ideas, and criteria for evaluating them and choosing those most worth pursuing. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, you should be able to: Distinguish between an idea and an opportunity. Explain Drucker's seven sources of opportunity. Apply idea generation and evaluation techniques.

search.c: Chapter 3: Opportunities and Idea Generation | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Many students come to this course with a "project idea" in mind and ask: Is it a good idea? The more precise question is: Is it an opportunity ? An idea is a picture in your mind of a product or service. It may be attractive and original, but it only becomes an opportunity when certain conditions exist in reality. These conditions can be summed up in four: Condition The question that tests it An example of its absence Real need Do people actually suffer from the problem you solve? An app for scheduling when to drink water, when people do not see this as a problem worth an app. Willingness to pay Are there enough people who will pay money or time for the solution? A service users love and use, but will not pay anything for. Right timing Are the market, technology and society ready now? An electronic payment service before smartphone use became widespread. Ability to execute Can you and your team deliver it with the resources available? An idea that needs a factory and complex licenses the team cannot obtain at the start. This means a good idea may not be an opportunity right now, and a very simple idea may be an excellent opportunity. An automatic reminder service for car maintenance and document renewals is not a brilliant idea, but it may be a real opportunity: a clear need that many people live with, willingness to pay among those who own more than one car, the right timing, and feasible execution.

search.c: Chapter 3: Opportunities and Idea Generation | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 3-2 Where Do Opportunities Come From? Drucker's Seven Sources
search.t: Peter Drucker argued that opportunities rarely come from sudden inspiration; they come from change . Every change in society, the market or knowledge opens a gap that a venture can fill. He identified seven sources of change, ordered from the easiest and least risky to the hardest: 1. The unexpected A success you did not plan, a failure you did not expect, or a sudden outside event. These surprises are the easiest source of opportunity, but many people ignore them because they do not fit their plans. Example: an online store for desert camping gear noticed that a "ready weekend trip bundle" it had listed as a trial outsold individual products. That is a sign customers are buying "a hassle-free trip," not just equipment. 2. Incongruity A gap between what is and what ought to be, or between what people expect and what they get. Example: a service people need often and pay for, yet the experience is poor, such as home maintenance appointments that nobody keeps. This incongruity is an opportunity for whoever offers the same service with reliability and clarity. 3. Process need A weak link inside a procedure or workflow that holds up everything before and after it. Example: a procedure that has become fully digital except for one step requiring a stamped paper; or a fast-food restaurant that is quick at everything except payment at peak times. Whoever fixes that link delivers a lot of value. 4. Changes in industry or market structure When the way an entire sector works changes, opportunities arise for newcomers, because established firms are slow to adapt. Example: the shift of shopping online created demand for packaging services, professional product photography, and online store management for traditional shops. 5. Demographic changes Changes in population size, age, education, and where people live and work. These are among the clearest sources of opportunity because they can be measured and anticipated. Example: a society with a large share of young people needs entertainment, education and fitness services, while one with a growing number of older people needs home care and accessible transport. More women entering the workforce has created demand for childcare and healthy ready meals. 6. Changes in perception and values When what people care about and value changes, even if the facts themselves have not. Example: growing interest in health and natural food created a market for organic products and specialized gyms. Concern for the environment created a market for recycling and sustainable products. 7. New knowledge Scientific discoveries and new technologies. This is the most exciting source, but also the hardest and riskiest, because turning new knowledge into a product takes a long time and needs other complementary technologies and knowledge. Example: today's AI tools open opportunities in education, customer service, translation and analysis, but succeeding with a venture in this area takes more than just using the technology. Application: when looking for an opportunity, do not start with "What venture do I want?" Ask instead: "What has changed around me in recent years? And who has been affected by this change and is not yet well served?"

search.c: Chapter 3: Opportunities and Idea Generation | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 3-3 Where Do You Start as a Student?
search.t: Alongside Drucker's sources, there are practical entry points a student can start from today: Your daily problems : the best ideas often start with a problem you live with yourself, because you understand it from the inside and know its real pain. But be careful: you must then check that others suffer from it too. Your field of study : a nursing student sees problems in the hospital that others do not, an education student knows what teachers struggle with, an engineering student knows the gaps in construction and maintenance. Knowledge of your field is a competitive advantage. People's complaints : search social media for phrases such as "I wish there were," "I'm tired of" and "does anyone know where," and read negative reviews of existing services. Every recurring complaint points to a gap. Trends : what is growing now? Tools such as Google Trends show what people search for most, and how that changes over time. Transferring and adapting an idea : a model that worked in another city, country or sector: could it work in your setting after adapting it to the local culture and needs? Improving what exists : you do not have to invent something new. It is enough to make what exists cheaper, faster, easier, closer, more attractive, or better suited to a specific group.

search.c: Chapter 3: Opportunities and Idea Generation | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Generating ideas is a skill with tools, not a matter of waiting for inspiration. The first rule in all of these tools is: separate generating from evaluating . While generating ideas, do not judge them, because early criticism kills ideas before they mature and makes people stop contributing. Evaluation comes later. 1. Brainstorming Developed by Alex Osborn in the mid-twentieth century, it rests on four rules: no criticism during the session, quantity before quality, welcome unusual ideas, and build on others' ideas. In practice: set a clear question, give the team a fixed time (ten minutes, for example), write each idea on a separate sticky note, then group them when time is up. 2. Reverse brainstorming Instead of asking "How do we solve the problem?", ask "How do we make it worse?" This question frees people from the fear of being wrong and produces many ideas quickly. Then reverse each bad idea to reach a solution. Example: "How do we make waiting at the clinic worse for patients?" → "Don't tell them when their turn will come." Reversed: "Send them a message with the approximate time of their turn so they can move around freely." 3. Mind mapping Write the topic in the center of the page (for example, "the patient's journey through the hospital"), then branch out to the main aspects (booking, arrival and parking, waiting, examination, pharmacy, follow-up), then branch from each aspect into its details and problems. The map helps you see connections between ideas and discover problems you had not thought of. 4. SCAMPER A list of seven questions developed by Bob Eberle, building on Osborn's work. You apply it to an existing product or service to generate new ideas from it. Each letter stands for a question: Letter Question Example for "a phone repair shop" S: Substitute What if we replaced part of the service, its materials or who provides it? Instead of the customer coming to the shop, we collect the device from their home or office and return it. C: Combine What if we combined it with another service? Repair + data transfer + screen protection in one bundle. A: Adapt What successful idea from another field could be adapted here? The "tracking" system of shipping companies: the customer knows where their repair has reached. M: Modify What if we enlarged, shrank, or changed the form or timing? A temporary loan phone the customer uses until the repair is done. P: Put to another use Could it serve another customer or purpose? Maintaining small companies' staff devices under a monthly contract. E: Eliminate What could be removed to make it simpler or cheaper? Eliminate waiting in the shop: a fixed pickup appointment. R: Reverse What if we reversed the order or the roles? Instead of selling repairs after a breakdown, sell a protection subscription before it. 5. The Five Whys A technique developed at Toyota to analyze the causes of problems. You ask "Why?" several times in a row until you reach the root cause instead of the visible symptom. Example: Why is the dental clinic losing part of its income? → Because many patients miss their appointments. Why do they miss them? → Because they forget the appointment. Why do they forget? → Because the appointment is booked weeks ahead and no reminder reaches them. Why does no reminder reach them? → Because the receptionist is busy, and reminders are done by phone, manually. Why is it manual? → Because the booking system does not send automatic messages. Now the opportunity changes: the problem is not "patients are unreliable" but "there is no automatic reminder," and the solution may be very simple and could be offered to many clinics. 6. "How might we…?" A phrasing used in design thinking that turns a problem into an open question inviting solutions. Instead of "Older people can't use government apps," you say: "How might we help older people complete their online transactions on their own, with confidence?" search.s: 3-5 Evaluating Ideas and Choosing the Best
search.t: After generating dozens of ideas, you need a systematic way to choose which ones deserve follow-up. The simplest way is to put the ideas in a table and score each from 1 to 5 on a set of criteria: Criterion Question What raises the score? Value Does it solve a painful or recurring problem? A problem people face often and look for a solution to Demand Are there enough customers? Will they pay? Many customers who pay today for worse solutions Feasibility Can we deliver it with our resources and skills? A simple version can be started within weeks Distinctiveness What makes it better than the alternatives? A clear advantage the customer notices immediately All parties satisfied Does everyone win: the customer, the entrepreneur, the service provider and the partner? The customer pays an amount they see as fair, and it is enough for every party to earn what they deserve (see Chapter 6) Growth Can it get bigger? It can be taken to other places or groups Team fit Are we excited about it and qualified to deliver it? It connects to our field and interests Some criteria can carry more weight. "Value" is the most important, because an idea that does not solve a real problem will not be rescued by any other criterion. Next comes "all parties satisfied," because many ideas customers love fall apart because they are exhausting or loss-making for whoever delivers them, as we will see with numbers in Chapter 6. Remember that this evaluation is preliminary and based on the team's estimates; the real verdict comes from customers in the chapters ahead.

search.t: 4 Chapter 4 Creativity and Innovation Innovation is the fuel that sets an entrepreneurial venture apart. But it is often confused with creativity, and sometimes reduced to "inventing a new product." In this chapter we clarify the difference between the two concepts, classify innovation by type and degree, and explain how new things spread among people, and why that matters to a venture owner. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, you should be able to: Distinguish between creativity and innovation. Classify innovation by type and degree. Explain the innovation adoption curve and why it matters to a venture.

search.c: Chapter 4: Creativity and Innovation | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 4-1 Creativity and Innovation: Related but Different
search.t: The two words are sometimes used to mean the same thing, but distinguishing them is essential for understanding entrepreneurship. Creativity is the ability to generate ideas that are new and useful. Researchers agree that a creative idea needs two conditions together: it must be novel (original, unfamiliar) and appropriate (useful, workable, solving a problem). A new idea that is not useful is mere oddity; a useful idea that is not new is repetition. Innovation is turning a creative idea into a product, service or way of working that people actually use and that adds value for them. The Oslo Manual, the international reference the OECD uses to measure innovation, defines it as a new or improved product or process that differs significantly from what came before and has been made available to users or brought into use . The difference in one sentence: creativity is when the idea occurs to you; innovation is when the idea reaches people and changes something in their lives. A brilliant idea in your notebook is creativity; when people use it, it becomes innovation. So a person can be very creative without being innovative, because they never complete the road to execution. And someone else may innovate successfully with a moderately creative idea, because they mastered execution and understood the customer. Entrepreneurship needs both: creativity to generate the idea, and innovation to turn it into value.

search.c: Chapter 4: Creativity and Innovation | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: When we talk about innovation, a new product comes to mind, such as a phone or a device. But innovation can happen in any part of a venture, and many of the most successful innovations did not change the product itself; they changed the way it is delivered or sold. 1. Product innovation A new product, or a clear improvement of an existing one in its function, quality or ease of use. Example: a water bottle that reminds you to drink with a small light, or an abaya made from fabric suited to summer heat. 2. Service innovation A new way of delivering a service, or of the customer's experience of it. Example: booking a barber appointment through a link, with a notification ten minutes before your turn, instead of waiting in the shop. The service itself (the haircut) has not changed, but the customer's experience has changed completely. 3. Process innovation A new method of production or internal operation that makes the venture faster, cheaper or more accurate, which the customer may not notice directly. Example: a kitchen that preps its basic ingredients in advance in an organized way, cutting order preparation time in half. 4. Business model innovation A new way of making money or of distributing value among the parties. It is one of the strongest types of innovation because it is hard to copy. Examples: a monthly subscription instead of paying each time, "buy now, pay later" in interest-free installments, or a platform that connects service providers with customers and takes a commission instead of employing them. 5. Marketing innovation A new way of presenting, packaging or pricing a product, or of reaching the customer. Example: a small farm that sells its produce in a weekly box with a card telling the story of the harvest, instead of selling wholesale at the market. 6. Social innovation New solutions to social problems, whose first goal is to improve people's lives. Example: a platform that connects young volunteers with older people in the neighborhood to help them with errands and online transactions.

search.c: Chapter 4: Creativity and Innovation | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Besides the type of innovation, we ask: how much change does it bring? Innovation is usually classified into three degrees: 1. Incremental innovation Small, continuous improvements to an existing product or service: a better camera in the new phone model, or a new flavor of a familiar product. Its risk is low, and its return is limited but relatively assured. Most innovation in the world is of this kind. 2. Radical innovation A major change that creates a new category of products or changes the way an entire sector works, such as the arrival of the smartphone itself, or the shift from in-store selling to e-commerce. Its risk is high and its cost large, but its impact is wide. 3. Disruptive innovation This concept was coined by Clayton Christensen, a management professor at Harvard, in The Innovator's Dilemma (1997). It is not a synonym for "big innovation"; it describes a specific pattern: The disruptive product starts out simple and lower in quality than the products of the major companies, but it is cheaper or easier . At first it serves a segment the major companies neglect : customers who cannot afford the expensive product, or do not need all its features. The major companies ignore it because it looks unprofitable and unimportant to their current customers. The product improves gradually until it becomes "good enough" for the major companies' own customers, and takes them away. The "dilemma" is that the major companies do not fail because they are badly managed, but because they do what is supposedly right: they listen to their current customers and focus on their most profitable products. That is exactly what makes them ignore the threat coming from below. The Kodak lesson: for decades Kodak was the leading name in photographic film. In 1975 one of its engineers, Steven Sasson, built an early prototype of a digital camera. But the first digital camera was slow and its pictures were poor, and the film business was very profitable, so the company hesitated to push the new technology forward so as not to compete with its own winning product. Digital cameras improved quickly, then smartphones arrived, the film business collapsed, and Kodak filed for bankruptcy in 2012. This is not the story of a company that did not know the technology, but of a company that knew it and did not dare disrupt itself.

search.s: 4-4 How Does Innovation Spread? The Adoption Curve
search.t: Sociologist Everett Rogers studied how new ideas and products spread through society, and published his theory in Diffusion of Innovations (1962; fifth edition 2003). He found that people do not adopt something new at the same time, but fall into five groups according to how quickly they adopt: Group Approximate share Characteristics What convinces them? Innovators 2.5% Love trying new things for their own sake, and tolerate flaws and risk Novelty itself Early adopters 13.5% Opinion leaders, looking for an advantage or a solution to a problem they feel acutely Clear benefit and the chance to stand out Early majority 34% Practical; wait for others to try it and for the product to prove itself Evidence and recommendations from people they trust Late majority 34% Skeptical; adopt once the product is common or necessary Social pressure and lower risk Laggards 16% Attached to the traditional; resist change Often adopt only when no alternative remains The chasm (Moore) Innovators 2.5% Early adopters 13.5% Early majority 34% Late majority 34% Laggards 16% Time → Figure: Rogers's innovation adoption curve, with the chasm Moore identified between early adopters and the early majority. Why does this matter to a venture owner? Because a common mistake is for a venture to target "everyone" from the start. The right approach is to look first for innovators and early adopters: people who feel the problem acutely and are willing to try a new solution even if it is not complete. They give you the first feedback and talk about you to others. Geoffrey Moore added an important observation in Crossing the Chasm (1991): between early adopters and the early majority lies a chasm into which many products fall. Early adopters accept an unfinished product because they like experimenting, but the majority wants a complete, reliable, proven product. To cross the chasm, a venture needs to focus on one specific segment of the majority, win it over completely, and then move on from it to others.

search.s: 4-5 What Makes People Adopt an Innovation?
search.t: Rogers identified five characteristics of the innovation itself that make people adopt it faster. You can use them as a checklist for your idea: Relative advantage : is it clearly better than what people use now? Compatibility : does it fit people's values, habits and needs? (A service that ignores cultural sensitivities will meet resistance however useful it is.) Simplicity : is it easy to understand and use? Trialability : can people try it at low cost before committing? (This is why free trials work.) Observability : can people see its results in others? (A product that is seen and talked about spreads faster.)

Innovation ranges from incremental improvement to radical change, and disruptive innovation can bring down leading companies. People adopt new things in stages, and early adopters are the starting point for any venture.

search.t: 5 Chapter 5 Understanding the Customer and the Market I have often seen ventures built on their owners' picture of what people need, only for them to be surprised that customers do not behave as expected. In this chapter we present the customer discovery method and the rules of a good interview, then explain market segmentation, estimating market size realistically, and analyzing competitors and alternatives. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, you should be able to: Apply the principles of customer discovery and interviewing. Define a customer segment and describe the target customer. Estimate market size and analyze competitors.

search.c: Chapter 5: Understanding the Customer and the Market | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: The most common mistake people with new ideas make is building their venture on their personal assumptions: "I need this service, so everyone needs it," or "This idea makes sense, so people will buy it." That assumption may be right, or it may be completely wrong. The only way to find out is to go to people and talk with them. This is the idea behind the customer discovery method developed by Steve Blank, entrepreneur and Stanford professor. He sums it up in a famous phrase: "There are no facts inside the building, so get out of the building." He means that everything a team writes in its office about the customer (who they are, what their problem is, how much they will pay) is nothing but hypotheses (testable guesses), and they only become facts after being tested with the customers themselves. Customer discovery follows clear steps: Write down your hypotheses : Who is the customer? What problem do they have? How do they solve it now? Why is the current solution not enough? Test the problem hypothesis first : does the problem really exist, and with the severity you think? Do not talk about your solution at this stage. Test the solution hypothesis : once you are sure of the problem, present your solution (as a simple prototype) and watch the reaction. Adjust or pivot : based on what you have learned, revise your hypotheses and repeat.

search.c: Chapter 5: Understanding the Customer and the Market | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 5-2 How to Conduct a Good Interview
search.t: You might think interviewing is easy: ask people what they think of your idea. The problem is that people usually try to be nice . Ask a friend "Do you like my idea?" and they will say yes to please you; ask someone "Would you buy this product if it existed?" and they will say maybe, because promising something in the future costs them nothing. You come out of your interviews convinced that everyone wants your idea, and discover at launch that nobody buys. Rob Fitzpatrick tackled this problem in The Mom Test , named that way because your mother is the person most likely to flatter you and say your idea is wonderful. His core rule: ask questions that a person cannot flatter you on even if they want to . Three rules achieve this: Rule 1: Talk about their life, not your idea Instead of explaining your idea and asking for their opinion, ask about their experience with the problem. When you talk about your idea, the conversation turns into politeness; when you talk about their life, it turns into information. Rule 2: Ask about the specific past, not the hypothetical future Questions about the future ("Would you use…?", "How much would you pay…?") give you wishes. Questions about the past ("The last time this happened, what did you do?") give you real behavior. If someone says they suffer from the problem a lot but have never looked for a solution, the problem is not painful enough. Rule 3: Listen more than you talk In a good interview the customer talks most of the time. Write down their words exactly as they say them, because they will help you later in marketing and pitching, and pay attention to emotions: annoyance, hesitation, enthusiasm. Weak question Why it is weak Better question Do you like the idea of an app for booking sports fields? It asks for an opinion, so it gets flattery The last time you wanted to play with friends, how did you book the field? Would you use the app if we launched it? It asks about the future, and promises are easy What is the hardest part of the current booking process? How much would you pay for the service? A hypothetical number that commits no one How much do you pay now to book? Have you tried another way? Don't you find the current booking tiring? A leading question that imposes the answer How would you describe the current booking experience? Another useful question is about frequency : "How many times have you needed this service in the past three months?" A problem that recurs every week is very different from one that comes up once a year, both in the size of demand and in the revenue model that suits it. Whom should you interview? Do not settle for your friends; they flatter you and are similar to you. Interview people who actually live the problem, from different backgrounds. At the end of each interview ask: "Do you know someone else who faces this problem?" This leads you to real customers. And look for commitment as stronger evidence than words: the person gives you extra time, introduces you to others, pays in advance, or asks to be told when the service launches. How many interviews are enough? There is no magic number, but after a number of interviews you will notice the answers starting to repeat. In this course we ask for at least five interviews, which is enough to find out whether your core assumptions are right.

search.s: 5-3 Market Segmentation and Choosing the Target Customer
search.t: There is no product "for everyone." Even products everyone uses, like water and phones, are offered by companies in different forms to different groups. Market segmentation is dividing potential customers into groups with similar needs and behavior, so that each group can be served in a way that suits it. The best-known bases for segmentation are four: Basis Example variables Applied example Demographic Age, gender, income, education, marital status, occupation Working mothers, or recent retirees Geographic City, neighborhood, region, type of place (urban, rural) Residents of new neighborhoods far from the city center Behavioral Purchase frequency, loyalty, buying method, occasion People who order food more than three times a week Psychographic and needs-based Lifestyle, values, interests, the job to be done Fitness enthusiasts looking for high-protein meals After segmenting, you choose one target segment to start with. Choose one that is large enough to sustain you, feels the problem acutely, is reachable by you, and is not well served by competitors. Starting with a narrow segment is not weakness but focus; serving a small group excellently is better than serving everyone averagely. Customer persona A persona describes a typical customer who represents your target segment as if they were a real person: a name, an age, a daily routine, problems and motivations. Its benefit is that when the team makes a decision it asks "Does this suit Sarah?" rather than the vague "Does this suit customers?" It is built from interview findings, not from imagination. Example persona: "Abu Salman, 46, owns two auto parts shops with five employees. At the end of every month he spends hours gathering paper invoices from the drawer, trying to work out whether he made or lost money. He does not trust software much, because he tried one and did not understand it. He pays a freelance accountant every quarter to prepare what the authorities require, but does not get a clear picture of his shops from it. What worries him most is discovering a loss too late. He says: 'I want someone to tell me at the end of the month, in simple words: you earned this much, and you lost on that.'" Notice how this persona reveals things the label "small shop owners" does not: he does not want complex software, he is currently paying for an inadequate solution, and what he really wants is reassurance and clarity , not the accounts themselves. Jobs to be Done Clayton Christensen and his colleagues developed a theory that people do not buy products; they "hire" them to get a job done in their lives. In the best-known example, a company studying why people bought a certain drink early in the morning discovered that many bought it to keep them company on the long commute and keep them full until noon. The "job" was not "drinking something tasty" but "making a boring commute better." That changes your view of competitors: the drink's competitor is not only another drink, but a banana, a muffin, and a podcast. When you understand the real job, you understand what you need to improve. An employee buying morning coffee on the way to work may not necessarily want "coffee," but "to start the day focused and energetic." A shop owner who pays an accountant does not want "accounting entries," but "to know whether the shop is profitable." This opens up wider alternatives and ideas.

search.c: Chapter 5: Understanding the Customer and the Market | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: The question any investor or panel will ask you: "How big is your market?" Market size is usually estimated at three nested levels: Level Meaning Example: a simple monthly bookkeeping service for small shops Total addressable market (TAM) Total potential demand if you won every possible customer All small businesses in Saudi Arabia that need to keep their books Serviceable available market (SAM) The part your model can actually reach Small retail shops in your city that you can serve with your team, language and approach Serviceable obtainable market (SOM) The realistic share you expect to win in the near term The number of shops you expect to actually subscribe in the first year, given your team's capacity and trial results The more accurate way to estimate is bottom-up : start from a small unit that can be verified, then multiply. Example: the number of retail shops in the neighborhoods you can reach (from a field count or chamber of commerce data) × the share without a regular accountant (from interviews) × the share willing to subscribe × the annual subscription fee. The weak way is top-down with no logic: "Saudi Arabia has so many million people, and if 1% of them buy, we will earn this much." That number convinces no one, because it does not answer the important question: why would these people buy from you in particular, and how will you reach them?

search.c: Chapter 5: Understanding the Customer and the Market | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Competition is not only whoever offers the same product, but anything the customer could choose instead of you to get the same job done. So competition is divided into three levels: Direct competitors : offer the same solution to the same customer. (Accounting offices offering a monthly service to shops.) Indirect competitors : offer a different solution to the same need. (Off-the-shelf accounting software, and the freelance accountant who comes every quarter.) Alternatives : what people do now, even if it is a primitive solution or "nothing." (A paper notebook, one of the children, or relying on memory.) When a student says "My idea has no competitors," it usually means one of two things: either they have not searched well, or people do not need this solution at all. The presence of competitors is a sign that a market exists; what matters is knowing what makes you different from them. To organize the comparison, make a simple table: competitors in the columns, criteria that matter to the customer in the rows (price, speed, proximity, quality, ease), then rate each competitor. The gaps where you can stand out will appear. SWOT analysis A common tool for organizing a picture of the venture in four boxes: Positive Negative Internal (about you and your team) Strengths : what you have and do better than others Weaknesses : the resources or skills you lack External (about the market and environment) Opportunities : market changes you can benefit from Threats : competitors, regulations or changes that could hurt you The real value of the analysis is not in filling the boxes, but in the next questions: How do I use my strengths to seize the opportunities? And how do I address my weaknesses before a threat exploits them?

search.t: Everything we know about the customer before talking with them is a hypothesis that needs testing. A good interview asks about the specific past and the customer's life, not their opinion of your idea. The market is divided into segments, from which a clear target customer is chosen and described with a persona. The market is estimated at three levels, calculated bottom-up with realistic numbers. Competition includes direct and indirect competitors and the alternatives people use now.

search.t: 6 Chapter 6 The Business Model Two similar products may succeed or fail depending on how each makes money and reaches its customers. This is what we call the business model. In this chapter we present the Business Model Canvas and its nine components, go deeper into the value proposition, and then review common revenue models. We end with one of the most important secrets of outstanding entrepreneurial ventures: a deal where every party wins, meaning a model in which the customer is satisfied and pays an amount that rewards the venture owner and everyone who works with them. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, you should be able to: Explain the nine components of the business model. Formulate the value proposition for your venture. Choose a suitable revenue model. Test your idea with the question "Does every party win?" and redesign it if they don't.

search.c: Chapter 6: The Business Model | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Alexander Osterwalder defines a business model as the logic by which a venture creates value, delivers it to its customers, and captures a return from it . In other words, it answers three connected questions: What value do we offer, and to whom? How do we deliver it to them? And how do we earn enough from it to cover our costs and make a profit? To see why the business model matters, consider how the same service, "getting around the city," can be offered through completely different business models: A company that sells cars: the customer pays for the car once and owns it. A rental company: the customer pays to use the car for some days and then returns it. A ride-hailing platform: the company owns no cars; it connects drivers with riders and takes a share of each trip. Public buses: the rider pays a nominal fare, and a government body subsidizes the service. The service is the same, but the way value is created and money is earned differs in each model. That is why researchers say that competition today is often between business models, not just between products.

search.c: Chapter 6: The Business Model | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: In Business Model Generation (2010), Osterwalder and Yves Pigneur designed a visual tool that summarizes a venture on a single page, divided into nine blocks. The tool spread through universities and incubators around the world because it forces the team to think about the whole venture and allows it to be revised quickly. The canvas is read in three parts: one side is about the customer and value (whom we serve and how we reach them), the other side is about operations (what we need in order to deliver the value), and the bottom is about money (where it comes from and where it goes). We will explain each block and apply it to one example that runs through the chapter: The example: "Baroda," an annual air-conditioner maintenance subscription for homes and shops, including scheduled visits before summer and in mid-summer, and priority for emergency breakdowns. 8 Key partners 7 Key activities 6 Key resources 2 Value proposition 4 Customer relationships 3 Channels 1 Customer segments 9 Cost structure 5 Revenue streams Operations Value Customer Figure: the Business Model Canvas (Osterwalder and Pigneur). The numbers suggest an order for filling it in: start with the customer and value, finish with costs. 1. Customer Segments The question: For whom are we creating value? Who are our most important customers? Here you define the groups the venture serves, with the precision explained in the previous chapter. A venture may serve one segment, or several segments with different needs. The rule is that each segment with a different need requires a different value proposition. In the example: two segments: (a) households whose air conditioners break down at the peak of the heat, leaving them waiting days for a technician; (b) owners of small shops and offices, who lose customers and staff comfort when the cooling fails. 2. Value Proposition The question: What problem do we solve for each segment? What benefit do we offer? Why would the customer choose us over the alternatives? This is the most important block on the canvas, because everything else serves it. A value proposition is not a list of product features but the benefit the customer feels . We expand on it in the fourth section. In the example: for households: "Your air conditioners are serviced before summer on a fixed date for a fixed annual price, so they don't break down in the worst of the heat." For shops: "Don't lose customers because of a broken air conditioner: regular maintenance, and an emergency visit within hours." 3. Channels The question: How do customers hear about us? How do they buy? How do we deliver the service? How do we support them after the sale? Channels are the points of contact between the venture and the customer at every stage of their journey: advertising, sales, delivery and after-sales service. They may be direct (your website, your shop, your team) or indirect (a distributor, a platform, a partner). In the example: awareness through neighborhood groups, real estate offices and residential compound managers; subscription and payment through a link; delivery through scheduled technician visits; after-sales support through a dedicated breakdown number. 4. Customer Relationships The question: What type of relationship do we build with each segment? How do we win customers, keep them and grow what they buy? The relationship may be personal (you know the customer by name), automated (an app with no human contact), or community-based (a group where customers interact with one another). Each type has a different cost and effect. In the example: a reminder before every visit, a photo report after maintenance showing the condition of each unit, priority for subscribers when breakdowns happen, and a discount on renewal. 5. Revenue Streams The question: What does the customer pay for? How do they pay? How much does each stream contribute to total revenue? Here you set the revenue model (sale, subscription, commission…) and the pricing method. We present revenu

search.s: 6-3 The Lean Canvas: A Version for Startups
search.t: Ash Maurya noticed that early-stage startups do not yet have clear partners or relationships, and that their biggest risk is building a solution to a problem that does not exist. In Running Lean he developed a modified version called the Lean Canvas , replacing four blocks: Block in the original canvas Replaced in the Lean Canvas by Reason Key Partners Problem: the customer's top three problems, and existing alternatives Because a startup must begin with the problem Key Activities Solution: the simplest solution to each problem Because the solution must connect directly to the problem Key Resources Key Metrics: the numbers that tell you whether the venture is making progress Because a startup needs to measure its learning Customer Relationships Unfair Advantage: what others cannot easily copy or buy Because a successful idea is copied quickly The two tools do not conflict: the Lean Canvas suits the idea and testing stage, and the original Business Model Canvas suits the stage when the model becomes clear and operations begin.

search.c: Chapter 6: The Business Model | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: The value proposition is the promise you make to the customer: why should they choose you? It is built by understanding three things about the customer: Jobs : what is the customer trying to get done? (Keep the home cool all summer without interruption.) Pains : what annoys, blocks or worries them? (A sudden breakdown, waiting days for a technician, not knowing the fair price, fear of an unreliable technician.) Gains : what outcomes do they hope for? (Peace of mind, a cost known in advance, a technician who knows their units.) You then design your product to be a pain reliever and a gain creator . This is the core of the Value Proposition Canvas, which Osterwalder and colleagues developed as a companion to the Business Model Canvas. Value usually comes from one or more of these sources: Source of value Example Saving time or effort The customer does not need to search for a technician or chase them Lowering cost Regular maintenance is cheaper than repairing major breakdowns Higher quality or performance Trained technicians and a photo report after every visit Convenience Visits are scheduled automatically without the customer having to remember Customization A plan based on the number and type of units Reducing risk A maintenance guarantee and a fixed price known in advance Social or emotional value Peace of mind and reassurance about the family in summer A template for writing the value proposition: "We help [customer] who struggles with [problem] to [desired outcome] through [solution]. Unlike [current alternative], we [what sets us apart]." In the example: "We help households whose air conditioners break down in the height of summer to enjoy a comfortable, uninterrupted summer, through a regular maintenance subscription with fixed dates and a fixed price. Unlike calling a technician after a breakdown, we prevent the breakdown before it happens and arrive on time."

search.c: Chapter 6: The Business Model | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: The revenue model is the way the customer pays. Choosing it affects everything: the price, the relationship with the customer, and cash flow. 1. Direct sale The customer pays for the product once and owns it. The simplest and clearest model, but it requires attracting the customer anew each time. (Shops, products.) 2. Subscription The customer pays a recurring amount (weekly, monthly, yearly) for continuing service. For the venture, it makes revenue predictable and regular and eases planning; for the customer, it is often cheaper and easier. But it requires value to stay high constantly, or the customer cancels. (Streaming platforms, gyms, "Baroda.") 3. Commission A platform connects two sides (seller and buyer, service provider and customer) and takes a share of each transaction. The platform does not need to own inventory or employ service providers, but it needs enough of both sides to work. (Delivery platforms, hotel booking.) 4. Freemium A free basic version attracts a large number of users, and a paid version with extra features is bought by some of them. Its success depends on the free version being useful enough to attract people, and the paid version tempting enough for them to pay. (Cloud storage apps, language learning apps.) 5. Advertising The service is free for the user, and advertisers pay to reach them. It needs a very large number of users to be profitable, so it rarely suits small ventures at the start. (Search engines, social media.) 6. Rental The customer pays for temporary use instead of ownership. It suits expensive things people need only occasionally. (Equipment rental, travel and camping gear.) 7. Licensing The venture sells the right to use its intellectual property (a brand, a technology, content, a design) to another party for a fee. (Enterprise software, brands.) More than one model can be combined, as in our example: an annual subscription, plus the sale of spare parts, plus one-off visits for non-subscribers.

search.c: Chapter 6: The Business Model | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 6-6 A Deal Where Every Party Wins
search.t: This section is among the most important in the book, because it addresses a mistake that recurs often in venture ideas: an idea that is wonderful for the customer, but exhausting or loss-making for whoever delivers it. 1. A venture has more than two parties When we think about a venture, we usually think about the customer alone: Will they like it? Will they use it? But every real venture has other parties: the entrepreneur , who must earn what their effort and money deserve; the workers , such as the technician, the courier and the driver, who must earn a fair income for their time; and the suppliers and partners , such as the supplier, the shop and the platform, for whom the partnership must be worthwhile. A sustainable venture is one from which every party comes away satisfied , not just by using it, but because the customer pays an amount they see as fair, and that amount rewards the entrepreneur and the other parties properly. If one party is "unhappy," the venture will not last long: a worker who does not earn enough leaves, a supplier who loses money withdraws, and an entrepreneur who works hard without profit eventually closes the venture, however happy the customers are. 2. The faces map One of the simplest ways to test any idea is to draw a face for each party: a happy face if they gain and are comfortable, and a sad face if they lose or are overburdened. Then look at the faces together: is everyone smiling? Consider these two examples: Party Idea: a mobile barber who comes to the customer's home Idea: a delivery platform connecting restaurants with customers (like HungerStation) Customer Likes having the barber come to them, but the price asked is too high, so they usually say: "Going to the shop is better for me." Receives exactly the order they chose, at a known time, without going out Service provider In the shop the barber serves many customers; going out to customers means fewer of them, higher costs and more scheduling problems The restaurant owner benefits because the platform markets the restaurant and connects it with customers it could not reach, without hiring couriers Courier — Starts work whenever they want, so they keep their freedom, and earn according to their effort Venture owner Cannot find a price that satisfies both the barber and the customer The company manages and connects the parties; its effort is small relative to the number of daily orders, so it earns on every order Result Not everyone is smiling Balanced , as long as the deal stays fair to each party Notice in the second example that the restaurant owner was not obliged to hire full-time couriers and carry their salaries and cars during slow hours, the courier was not bound to fixed working hours, the customer did not have to go anywhere, and the company neither cooked nor owned cars. Each party got what it wanted and gave what it could. 3. The value pie: why is one party unhappy? Researchers Adam Brandenburger and Harborne Stuart offer a simple and deep way to understand this, which can be summarized as follows: Value created by the venture = the most the customer is willing to pay − the least the service provider is willing to accept The least the provider will accept is their real cost, and that includes their time : what they would have earned had they used that time on other work. Picture this value as a pie divided among the parties: a slice for the customer (the difference between what they were willing to pay and what they actually paid, which is what makes them happy), a slice for the entrepreneur (profit), and a slice for the service provider and suppliers (what exceeds their costs). There are two cases: If the pie is large (the customer is willing to pay much more than the cost), each party can take a slice and everyone smiles. If the pie is small or negative (the real cost is higher than what the customer will pay), there is no price that makes everyone happy. Raise the price and the customer is unhappy; lower it and the pro

search.c: Chapter 6: The Business Model | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: The business model is the logic of creating value, delivering it and earning from it. The Business Model Canvas sums up a venture in nine components on a single page, and has a version for startups (the Lean Canvas). The value proposition answers the question: why would the customer choose us over the alternatives? Revenue models include sale, subscription, commission, freemium, advertising, rental and licensing. A sustainable venture satisfies all its parties: the customer pays an amount they see as fair, and it is enough for the entrepreneur, workers and partners to earn. If the real cost (including time) is higher than what the customer will pay, no price makes everyone happy, and the solution lies in changing the model, not the price. Among the secrets of balanced models: using idle resources, bundling demand, subscriptions, and an intermediary that saves everyone something.
