search.s: Chapter 7: Testing and Prototyping | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: 7 Chapter 7 Testing and Prototyping The greatest danger facing a new venture is spending its time and money building something nobody wants. That is why methods developed that treat a venture as a series of small experiments. In this chapter we present the lean startup method, the types of minimum viable product, the stages of design thinking, the concept of the pivot, and the role of AI tools in testing. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, you should be able to: Explain the lean startup method and the build–measure–learn loop. Choose the type of minimum viable product that suits your idea. Explain the stages of design thinking and the meaning of a "pivot."

search.c: Chapter 7: Testing and Prototyping | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Imagine a team that spent six months coding an app for booking football fields, spent a large sum on its design and development, launched it, and discovered that young people book fields by calling a field manager they know, and see no need for an app. The team could have discovered this in a single week had it tested before building. This story repeats itself often, and it is why methods emerged that treat a new venture differently: instead of planning at length and then executing, test small, learn fast, then decide . This chapter presents two complementary methods: the lean startup and design thinking.

search.c: Chapter 7: Testing and Prototyping | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Eric Ries set out this method in The Lean Startup (2011), drawing on Steve Blank's ideas about customer discovery and on Toyota's "lean production," which focuses on reducing waste. The core idea is that the biggest waste in new ventures is building something nobody wants . So the goal of a venture at the start should be validated learning : knowing, with evidence, what the customer actually wants. The build–measure–learn loop A lean venture works in a repeating loop, and the faster the loop, the faster the learning: Build : build the simplest version of your idea that lets you test a specific hypothesis. Do not build the whole product. Measure : put this version in front of real customers, and measure what they do , not what they say: How many signed up? How many ordered? How many came back a second time? Learn : compare the results with what you expected. Is the hypothesis right? If so, move on to the next hypothesis. If not, adjust or pivot. Product (MVP) Data Ideas Build Measure Learn The faster the loop, the faster you learn Figure: the build–measure–learn loop of the lean startup method (Ries). Start with a hypothesis Every experiment starts with a clearly written hypothesis, so that you know in advance what you are testing and when the experiment counts as a success. A useful template: "We believe that [customer] will [specific behavior] because [reason] . We will know we are right if [clear numerical measure] within [period] ." Example: "We believe that households in new neighborhoods will subscribe to annual maintenance of their air conditioners before summer, because they suffered breakdowns and waits for technicians last summer. We will know we are right if at least 15 of the 100 households we reach subscribe within two weeks." Notice that the hypothesis sets a number before the experiment. If only 3 households subscribe, you cannot say "the result is fairly good," because you decided in advance what success means.

search.c: Chapter 7: Testing and Prototyping | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: A minimum viable product is the simplest version of a product that lets you learn from real customers with the least effort and cost . The concept is often misunderstood: it is not a poor version of the final product, but an experiment designed to answer a question. It may need no coding or manufacturing at all. There are many kinds, listed here from the simplest to the most committed: 1. Paper or visual prototype You draw the app's screens or the service's stages on paper and ask the user to "use" them with a finger while you flip the pages. It quickly shows whether the user understands the idea and how to use it. Its cost is almost zero, and it takes an hour. 2. Landing page A simple web page that describes the service as if it already existed, with a "Register your interest" or "Reserve your spot" button. You post the link where your customers are and measure: How many people visited the page? How many signed up? The sign-up rate indicates real interest. Such a page can be built today with free tools and no coding. 3. Explainer video A short clip showing how the service will work. It is used when the product is hard to build but easy to explain. You publish it and measure engagement, questions and sign-up requests. 4. Concierge MVP You deliver the service manually, yourself, to a small number of customers, who know you are doing it by hand. Example: before building a delivery app, you take orders via WhatsApp and deliver them yourself to twenty customers for two weeks. You will learn what people actually order, when, and what annoys them, before writing a single line of code. 5. Wizard of Oz MVP The name comes from the story of the wizard who appears mighty and turns out to be an ordinary man behind a curtain. The customer sees an interface that looks automated or intelligent, but a person is working behind it by hand. Example: a "smart book recommendation" service where the customer fills in a form and receives recommendations within an hour, while a team member writes them personally. The difference from the concierge MVP is that the customer does not know the work is manual. 6. Pre-order You offer the product for sale before making it, and the customer pays in advance or commits to buy. This is the strongest possible evidence of demand, because paying is a real commitment with no politeness in it. Crowdfunding platforms rely on it. Type What it mainly tests Strength of evidence Paper prototype Understanding and ease of use Weak to medium Landing page and video Interest in the idea Medium Concierge and Wizard of Oz Actual use and operational details Strong Pre-order Willingness to pay Strongest When should I launch? A question students ask often: should I wait until the product is complete and perfect, or launch quickly? The answer lies in the idea of the minimum itself: don't wait for perfection. Launch the simplest version that is enough for the customer to try, then improve it with what you learn from real use. A product that waits for perfection may never reach anyone.

search.t: Design thinking is a problem-solving approach that puts the human being at the center of the process: it starts with a deep understanding of people's needs, feelings and behavior, then designs solutions with them and for them. It grew out of the way designers work, and was spread by the design firm IDEO and Stanford University's design institute (the d.school). Tim Brown, IDEO's chief executive, describes it as an approach that balances three things: what people desire, what is technically feasible, and what is commercially viable. Design thinking differs from the traditional way of solving problems in two respects: it does not jump to a solution before understanding the problem from the person's point of view, and it is non-linear , meaning the team moves between stages and returns to earlier ones whenever it learns something new. The Stanford d.school divides it into five stages, which we explain one at a time and apply to a single example: 1 Empathize Understand people 2 Define Frame the problem 3 Ideate Generate solutions 4 Prototype Make it tangible 5 Test Try and learn Going back to an earlier stage is part of the method Figure: the five stages of design thinking (Stanford d.school), which are not a straight line. The example: a team of students noticed that older people in their neighborhood struggle when visiting the hospital for regular follow-up appointments. Stage 1: Empathize The goal: to understand the people you are designing for: What do they do? What do they say? What do they feel? And what do they not say? How? Through three main means: Observation : watch people in their real environment without intervening. What do they do? Where do they stop? What confuses them? Interviews : talk with them about their experiences, with open questions about specific situations, as explained in Chapter 5. And ask "Why?" a lot. Immersion : go through the experience yourself. Make the follow-up journey the way an older person does. In the example: the team accompanied three older people to their appointments, and interviewed five others and their adult children. They noticed that an older person arrives an hour before the appointment for fear of being late, gets lost between departments, and that his son has to take time off work to accompany him; and that what bothers the older person most is not the waiting but the feeling of being a burden on his children. Output of the stage: observations and quotes from people, which the team sometimes organizes into an "empathy map" with four parts: What do they say? What do they do? What do they think? What do they feel? Stage 2: Define The goal: to turn the observations you gathered into a clear definition of the real problem from the person's perspective, not yours. How? The team gathers the observations and looks for recurring patterns and surprises, then writes a point-of-view statement in the form: "[User] needs [need] because [insight we discovered]." Then it turns it into a "How might we…?" question. In the example: the team noticed that the problem they assumed at first ("the wait is long") was not the real problem. They wrote: "An older person who visits the hospital regularly needs to go and return independently and with peace of mind, because he feels embarrassed about being a burden on his children." And the question: "How might we help older people attend hospital appointments independently, without worrying or wearing out their children?" Why does this stage matter? Because the definition of the problem determines the type of solutions. Had the team kept the definition "the wait is long," it would have designed a faster booking system, a solution that does not touch what really bothers the older person. Stage 3: Ideate The goal: to produce as many varied solutions as possible to the question you framed, before choosing. How? With the techniques from Chapter 3: brainstorming, reverse brainstorming and SCAMPER, with criticism postponed. The team is encouraged to propose bold

search.c: Chapter 7: Testing and Prototyping | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: When experiments show that part of your hypotheses is wrong, you face three options: persevere because the results are encouraging, pivot , or stop . A pivot, as Ries defines it, is a deliberate change in one part of the business model based on what you have learned, while keeping what has proven to work. The term comes from the basketball player who keeps one foot planted and moves the other to change direction. Common types of pivot include: Customer segment pivot : the product solves a real problem, but for a different customer than the one you targeted. (In the older people example: the paying customer is the son.) Problem pivot : the customer is right, but the problem that hurts them is different. Zoom-in pivot : one feature of your product is what people love, so you make it the whole product. Revenue model pivot : people want the product, but with a different way of paying (a subscription instead of a sale, for example). Channel pivot : the product is good, but the way of reaching the customer does not work. Well-known examples: Instagram began as an app called Burbn for checking in at places and sharing them, with many features. Its founders noticed that users used nothing in the app except photo sharing, so they removed everything else and focused on it (a zoom-in pivot). And Slack, the team communication tool, came out of an internal tool built by a company developing an online game that did not succeed; the company dropped the game and kept the tool.

search.c: Chapter 7: Testing and Prototyping | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Generative AI tools have become part of entrepreneurs' work today, and they save a great deal of time in the testing stages. You can use them to: Suggest interview questions and review your own to avoid leading questions. Summarize interview notes and draw out recurring patterns. Draft the text of a landing page, or design it. Generate additional ideas in a brainstorming session. Play the role of the "critic" looking for holes in your idea. But these tools have limits you need to know: What they say about your customers is a hypothesis based on general patterns, not evidence about your own customers. It cannot replace talking with people. They do not know your local environment and its details as you do. They may invent numbers, sources or facts that sound convincing but are wrong, so verify every piece of information you get. If they write your work for you, you will not learn the skill you came to learn. In a study I conducted with 123 university students from several disciplines (Alsamani, 2026), students applied a structured protocol for collaborating with generative AI tools for two weeks within an innovative business project. They reported that this collaboration helped them prepare deeper SWOT analyses and generate innovative ideas, and that among the most useful things they did were rephrasing prompts, asking for clarification, and questioning their projects' assumptions. The key word here is "structured": knowing what to ask the tool for, when and why, and remaining the one who makes the decisions. The practical rule: use AI as an assistant in developing and building ideas, not as a substitute for your thinking and for your own voice in writing.

search.c: Chapter 7: Testing and Prototyping | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: A new venture is an experiment whose aim is to learn as fast and cheaply as possible through the build–measure–learn loop. A minimum viable product is the simplest version that allows learning from real customers, and it takes many forms. Design thinking is a human-centered approach with five repeating stages. A pivot is a deliberate change based on evidence, not an escape from the venture. AI is an assistant in testing, and what it says about customers is a hypothesis that needs verifying.

search.c: Chapter 7: Testing and Prototyping | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani

search.s: Chapter 8: Marketing for New Ventures | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: 8 Chapter 8 Marketing for New Ventures An excellent product nobody knows about will not succeed, while an ordinary product with smart marketing may spread widely. But marketing in new ventures differs from marketing in large companies: the budget is small, the brand is unknown, and every customer matters. In this chapter we cover the foundations of marketing, from choosing the customer and positioning, to the marketing mix, the customer journey, digital marketing and measuring results. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, you should be able to: Apply the marketing mix and the segmentation, targeting and positioning process. Write a positioning statement for your venture. Build a simple digital marketing plan and measure its results.

search.c: Chapter 8: Marketing for New Ventures | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Many people reduce marketing to advertising or posting on social media, but advertising is a small part of it. Philip Kotler, one of the best-known authors in the field, defines marketing as the process of creating value for customers and building strong relationships with them, in order to capture value from them in return . In other words, marketing begins long before advertising: with understanding the customer, choosing whom to serve, designing an offer that suits them, delivering it, and then keeping them. Marketing conditions in a new venture differ from those in large companies: the budget is small, the brand is unknown, and customers do not trust something they have not tried. A new venture therefore needs focused, smart marketing more than broad, expensive marketing.

search.c: Chapter 8: Marketing for New Ventures | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Before deciding what to say and where to advertise, you must decide whom you are talking to, and how you want them to see you. This is the STP model, three consecutive steps: 1. Segmentation Dividing the market into groups with similar needs and characteristics, using the bases explained in Chapter 5: demographic, geographic, behavioral and psychographic. 2. Targeting Choosing the segment (or segments) you will focus on. The target is chosen with three questions: Is the segment large enough and profitable? Can we reach and serve it? Can we outperform competitors in it? Trying to target everyone makes your message generic and noticed by no one. 3. Positioning Positioning is the place you want your venture to occupy in the customer's mind relative to the alternatives . Al Ries and Jack Trout explained in their famous book Positioning that customers are exposed to thousands of messages, so they file products in their minds under a single simple word or idea: this one is "the cheapest," that one "the fastest," a third "the most luxurious." A venture that does not define its position is placed wherever the customer pleases, or forgotten. Positioning is usually defined by one main advantage, not a long list of features. This template helps you write a positioning statement: "For [target customer] who [need or problem] , [venture name] is the [product category] that [main benefit] . Unlike [main alternative] , it [reason it stands out] ." Example: "For shop owners who lose customers when the air conditioning fails, Baroda is a regular maintenance subscription that guarantees an emergency visit within hours. Unlike the technician you call after a breakdown, we prevent the breakdown before it happens and know your units." A positioning statement is not an advertising slogan to publish, but an internal compass for the team: every decision about pricing, design and advertising should be consistent with it.

search.c: Chapter 8: Marketing for New Ventures | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Once you have defined the customer and the positioning, you translate them into practical decisions about four elements, formulated by E. Jerome McCarthy in the 1960s and popularized by Kotler: 1. Product What exactly are we offering? This includes the product itself, its quality, design, packaging and name, and the services that accompany it. The most important question here is: what is the benefit, not the specification? A customer does not buy "a 20-liter waterproof backpack"; they buy "a bag that protects your laptop and books in the rain." That is why it is said that people do not buy a drill; they buy the hole in the wall. 2. Price How much does the customer pay, and how? Price is not just a number but a marketing message: a high price suggests quality and distinction, while a low price suggests economy and may suggest poor quality. Price must be consistent with positioning. We discuss pricing methods in detail in Chapter 9. 3. Place (distribution) Where and how does the customer get the product? In a shop, online, by delivery, or through a distributor. The rule is to be where your customer is, and to make getting your product as easy as possible. Every extra step the customer needs in order to buy reduces the number who complete the purchase. 4. Promotion How does the customer learn about your product and become convinced by it? This includes advertising, content, public relations, offers, personal selling and digital marketing. We expand on it in the fifth section. Extra elements for services Because a service cannot be touched before it is bought, researchers added three elements for service marketing, making the mix seven elements (7Ps): People : whoever delivers the service is part of it. The manner of the employee or courier makes or breaks the experience. Process : the steps of delivering the service: How does the customer book? How long do they wait? How do they pay? Every step is part of the experience. Physical evidence : what the customer sees and touches and uses to judge the quality of a service they cannot see: the cleanliness of the premises, the packaging, the website design, the uniform, the invoice.

search.c: Chapter 8: Marketing for New Ventures | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Customers do not buy in a single moment. They go through stages, from the first time they hear about you to becoming a regular customer who recommends you. Understanding these stages helps you see where you lose customers: Stage What happens A question for the venture Awareness The customer learns you exist for the first time Do our target customers even see us? Interest They want to know more Is our message clear, and does it speak to their problem? Evaluation They compare you with the alternatives Why would they choose us? Do we have evidence and trust (reviews, a trial)? Purchase They decide and pay Is buying easy? How many steps does it take? Experience They use the product or service Does the experience deliver on the promise? Repeat They come back to buy again What makes them come back? Recommendation They talk about you to others Is the experience worth talking about? Note that keeping a customer is much cheaper than attracting a new one, which is why marketing does not end at the sale; it starts there.

search.c: Chapter 8: Marketing for New Ventures | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 8-5 Digital Marketing for a New Venture
search.t: Digital platforms have let small ventures reach their customers at low cost, but they have also made competition for attention fierce. Here are some practical principles: 1. Focus on one or two channels Do not try to be on every platform with poor quality. Choose the platform where your target customer spends time, and master it. Gabriel Weinberg explains in Traction that most successful ventures grew at first through one main channel they discovered by experimenting. 2. Content before advertising Useful content builds trust before the sale: show the problem and how you solve it, behind-the-scenes work, real customer stories, and useful tips in your field. People follow those who help them, then buy from those they trust. 3. Short video Short video has become one of the most widespread forms of content on the platforms. It does not need professional equipment; clarity, honesty and a good idea matter more than filming quality. 4. Personal recommendation In close-knit societies like ours, buying decisions are strongly influenced by the opinions of relatives and friends. A satisfied customer who talks about you is more powerful than any advertisement. You can encourage this with an experience worth talking about, or with a referral program that rewards whoever brings in a new customer. 5. Micro-influencers Accounts with fewer followers who are interested in your field or in your city are often more useful, cheaper and more credible than celebrities. Make sure any collaboration with them is clearly disclosed, in compliance with regulations and out of respect for the audience. 6. Customer service is part of marketing A fast, polite reply and solving the problem when it happens create loyalty. A complaint handled well can turn an angry customer into one of your most loyal.

search.c: Chapter 8: Marketing for New Ventures | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: One advantage of digital marketing is that it can be measured. The most important metrics for a new venture are: Conversion rate : the share of those who completed a purchase out of those who viewed or visited. If 500 people visit your page and 25 buy, the conversion rate is 5%. Customer acquisition cost (CAC) : total marketing spend in a period ÷ the number of new customers in the same period. If you spend SAR 3,000 and gain 60 customers, the cost per customer is SAR 50. Customer lifetime value (LTV) : the average a customer pays over their whole relationship with you. If a customer buys a monthly subscription at SAR 100 and stays six months on average, their value is about SAR 600 in revenue. Retention rate : the share of customers who come back or renew. The basic rule: customer value must be clearly greater than the cost of acquiring the customer , or every new customer loses you money. In the example above, if customer value is SAR 600 and acquisition cost is SAR 50, the model is healthy. But if a customer buys once for SAR 40 and costs SAR 50 to acquire, the venture loses money with every customer.

search.c: Chapter 8: Marketing for New Ventures | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Marketing that succeeds over the long term rests on trust. So avoid exaggerated promises you cannot keep, fake reviews and ratings, undisclosed advertising presented as personal opinion, and hidden fees or conditions. Comply with the regulations governing advertising, e-commerce and consumer protection, and respect your customers' data and privacy. A reputation built in a year can be destroyed in a day, especially in a society where news travels fast.

search.c: Chapter 8: Marketing for New Ventures | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Marketing is understanding the need, designing an offer that meets it, delivering it to the customer and keeping them. Marketing starts with choosing the segment, then defining the positioning relative to the alternatives. The marketing mix: product, price, place and promotion, with people, process and physical evidence added for services. A new venture focuses on one or two channels, and measures customer acquisition cost and lifetime value.

search.s: Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Finance and Funding | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: 9 Chapter 9 Fundamentals of Finance and Funding Many students avoid the financial side, thinking it is for accountants. But its basics are simple, and knowing them is what separates a nice idea from a venture that survives. In this chapter we explain the types of costs, revenue and profit, contribution margin and the break-even point, pricing methods, the difference between profit and cash flow, and then the sources and stages of funding. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, you should be able to: Distinguish between start-up, fixed and variable costs. Calculate contribution margin and the break-even point. Distinguish between profit and cash flow, and know the sources and stages of funding.

search.c: Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Finance and Funding | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 9-1 Why Every Entrepreneur Needs Financial Basics
search.t: It is said that money is the language of business: every decision in a venture, from price to the number of employees to expansion, is ultimately translated into numbers. An entrepreneur does not need to be an accountant, but does need a clear grasp of a few basic concepts, because their absence is why many small ventures sell a lot and then close: their owners did not work out properly how much each product costs them, or how much they must sell to cover their costs. In this chapter we explain the concepts one after another and apply them to a single example, so you can see how they fit together: The example: "Hamsa," a small specialty coffee roastery that roasts its own beans and sells them in bags through an online store, shipping to customers in cities across Saudi Arabia.

search.c: Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Finance and Funding | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: The first step is knowing where the money goes. Costs in small ventures fall into three types, and confusing them is one of the most common mistakes: 1. Start-up (capital) costs Paid once when the venture starts, to get it ready to operate. They do not recur every month, but they can be large. They include: equipment and machines, fitting out the premises, designing the brand identity and logo, the first license, initial inventory, and the rent deposit. In the example: a small roasting machine and equipment (SAR 20,000), fitting out the premises (5,000), designing the identity and online store (4,000), and license and procedure fees (1,000). Total: SAR 30,000. 2. Fixed (operating) costs Recur every month and do not change with sales volume: you pay them whether you sell one bag or a thousand. They include: rent, fixed salaries, subscriptions (internet, software, platforms), average electricity and water, insurance, and loan installments. In the example: roastery rent (SAR 3,000), an assistant's salary (4,500), and electricity plus store and platform subscriptions (1,500). Total: SAR 9,000 a month. Don't forget your own salary. Many students count their employees' salaries and forget themselves, so the venture looks profitable when in fact it does not reward its owner for their time. If you will work in the venture, give yourself a reasonable salary within the fixed costs, then look again: is the venture still profitable? 3. Variable costs Linked to each unit sold : they rise as sales rise and fall as sales fall. They include: raw materials, packaging, payment gateway fees, delivery charges per order, and platform commission if any. In the example: green coffee beans (SAR 18 per bag), the bag and label (3), and shipping and payment fees (4). Total: SAR 25 per bag. How do you tell fixed from variable? Ask: if I sold nothing this month, would I still pay this cost? If yes, it is fixed; if no, it is variable. Some costs are mixed, like electricity, which has a fixed part and a part that grows with production; in small ventures it is enough to estimate it at its monthly average within fixed costs. Time is a cost too One of the costs most often overlooked by people with new ideas is time . If the service requires the provider to spend time on the road, waiting or setting up, the customer pays nothing for that time, but it reduces the number of customers who can be served in a day, raising the real cost per customer. So always ask: How many customers can the venture actually serve in a day? And look back at the mobile barber example in Chapter 6, where the barber needed more than double the shop price to earn the same income.

search.c: Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Finance and Funding | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Revenue is the money that comes into the venture from sales: unit price × number of units sold. It is not profit, but the money before any cost is deducted. Costs are then deducted in stages, and the table that shows this is called the income statement (or profit and loss statement). Suppose Hamsa sells a bag for SAR 55 and sold 400 bags this month: Item Calculation Amount (SAR) Revenue 400 × 55 22,000 (−) Variable costs 400 × 25 10,000 = Total contribution margin 22,000 − 10,000 12,000 (−) Fixed costs Rent + salary + services 9,000 = Operating profit 12,000 − 9,000 3,000 Statutory obligations such as zakat or tax, depending on the business's status, are then deducted from operating profit, leaving net profit . The profit margin is profit as a share of revenue: in the example 3,000 ÷ 22,000 ≈ 14%, meaning the venture keeps about SAR 14 of every SAR 100 it sells, before statutory obligations.

search.c: Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Finance and Funding | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 9-4 Contribution Margin and the Break-even Point
search.t: These are the two most important concepts in this chapter, because they answer every entrepreneur's question: How much must I sell so I don't lose money? Unit contribution margin The difference between the selling price of a unit and its variable cost: Unit contribution margin = selling price − variable cost per unit In the example: 55 − 25 = SAR 30 It is called a "contribution margin" because every bag you sell "contributes" SAR 30: first to covering fixed costs, and once they are all covered, everything beyond is profit. The break-even point The sales volume at which revenue equals total costs, so the venture neither profits nor loses: Break-even point (units) = monthly fixed costs ÷ unit contribution margin In the example: 9,000 ÷ 30 = 300 bags a month , or 10 bags a day on average. Let us check: at 300 bags, revenue = 300 × 55 = SAR 16,500, and costs = (300 × 25) + 9,000 = 7,500 + 9,000 = SAR 16,500. Profit is zero. Monthly sales Total contribution margin Fixed costs Result 200 bags 6,000 9,000 Loss of 3,000 300 bags 9,000 9,000 Break-even (zero) 400 bags 12,000 9,000 Profit of 3,000 600 bags 18,000 9,000 Profit of 9,000 0 5,000 10,000 15,000 20,000 25,000 30,000 0 100 200 300 400 500 600 Break-even: 300 bags Loss Profit Revenue (55 × bags) Total costs (9,000 + 25 × bags) Fixed costs 9,000 Bags sold per month SAR Figure: the break-even point for the Hamsa roastery. Below 300 bags revenue is under costs (a loss); beyond it, every extra bag adds SAR 30 to profit, as long as the price and variable cost stay the same. What do you do with the break-even point? Ask: Is selling 10 bags a day realistic? How many orders do we actually expect, based on our experiments? If the number is far from reality, you have three options: raise the price (if the value allows it), lower the variable cost (a cheaper supplier, simpler packaging, consolidated shipping), or lower the fixed costs (smaller premises, or renting time on an existing roastery at first instead of buying a machine). Try these scenarios in the break-even calculator in the toolbox. Where do start-up costs go? Notice that we did not include the SAR 30,000 in start-up costs in the monthly break-even calculation. The reason is that it is not a monthly cost but an amount paid once, recovered from profits after passing the break-even point. The time needed to recover it is called the payback period : Payback period = start-up costs ÷ monthly profit If the venture sells 400 bags a month (profit SAR 3,000): 30,000 ÷ 3,000 = 10 months . If it sells 600 bags (profit 9,000): 30,000 ÷ 9,000 ≈ 3.3 months . A common mistake is for a student to divide the start-up costs by the contribution margin and call the result "the break-even point." That result tells you how many units you need to recover the start-up costs, but it ignores the fixed costs you pay every month.

search.c: Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Finance and Funding | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 9-5 Profit Margin and Net Profit: The Coffee Cup Example
search.t: Many people confuse three closely related terms: contribution margin , net profit and profit margin . To make the differences clear, let us take the simplest venture possible: a small café that sells only one product, a single type of coffee at a single price, so the calculation is easy and every concept stands out. The example: a café that sells only one type of coffee, at SAR 15 a cup. The variable cost of a cup is SAR 6 (coffee 3, milk 1.5, cup and lid 1, payment fee 0.5). Its fixed costs are SAR 15,000 a month (rent 6,000, two employees' salaries 8,000, electricity and subscriptions 1,000). 1. Contribution margin: what one cup leaves behind Contribution margin per cup = 15 − 6 = SAR 9 . This is not profit yet; it is what remains of the cup after its variable cost, and it goes first to covering the rent and salaries. The break-even point = 15,000 ÷ 9 ≈ 1,667 cups a month , about 56 cups a day. 2. Net profit: what is actually left at the end of the month Suppose the café sold 2,000 cups this month: Item Calculation Amount (SAR) Revenue 2,000 × 15 30,000 (−) Variable costs 2,000 × 6 12,000 = Total contribution margin 2,000 × 9 18,000 (−) Fixed costs Rent + salaries + services 15,000 = Operating profit 18,000 − 15,000 3,000 (−) Statutory obligations (such as zakat), assumed 300 = Net profit 3,000 − 300 2,700 Notice the large difference: every cup "contributes" SAR 9, but the net amount left from each cup this month is 2,700 ÷ 2,000 = only SAR 1.35 . If we break down the price of a cup (SAR 15), it divides like this: SAR 6 variable cost, SAR 7.5 its share of fixed costs (15,000 ÷ 2,000), SAR 0.15 statutory obligations, and SAR 1.35 net profit. That is why it is wrong to say "I make SAR 9 on every cup." 3. Profit margin: profit as a share of sales Net profit margin = net profit ÷ revenue . In the example: 2,700 ÷ 30,000 = 9% , meaning the café keeps SAR 9 of every SAR 100 it sells. This ratio is useful because it allows comparison between two ventures of different sizes, or between two months of the same venture. 4. What stays fixed, and what changes with sales? If the number of cups sold changes, while the price and costs stay the same: Cups per month Revenue Operating profit Average profit per cup Profit margin What each extra cup adds 1,000 15,000 −6,000 −6 −40% 9 2,000 30,000 3,000 1.5 10% 9 3,000 45,000 12,000 4 about 27% 9 4,000 60,000 21,000 5.25 35% 9 The last column is constant: every extra cup adds SAR 9, before the break-even point and after it; before it, the 9 goes to covering fixed costs, and after it, it becomes profit. But the average profit per cup and the profit margin rise with sales, because the same fixed costs are spread over more cups. However much sales grow, the profit margin before obligations will never exceed 60% (9 ÷ 15), because that is the most a cup leaves after its variable cost. The same happens at Hamsa: every extra bag adds SAR 30, and the average profit per bag rises from SAR 7.5 at 400 bags to SAR 15 at 600 bags. When does the margin not stay fixed? The calculation above assumes that the price and the variable cost do not change, an assumption that holds within a certain range of sales. In reality the margin may change for three reasons: (1) a supplier discount for buying larger quantities, which lowers the variable cost and raises the margin; (2) cutting the price or running offers to sell more, which lowers the margin; (3) a jump in fixed costs beyond a certain point, such as the café needing a third employee or a second machine, which creates a new break-even point. So redo the calculation whenever any of these changes.

search.c: Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Finance and Funding | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Pricing is one of the hardest and most consequential decisions in a venture, because changing the price by a few riyals can change profit substantially. If Hamsa raised its price from SAR 55 to 60, the contribution margin would rise from 30 to 35, and the break-even point would fall from 300 to about 258 bags. There are four main pricing methods: 1. Cost-plus pricing You calculate the unit cost, then add a profit percentage. Example: a variable cost of SAR 25 + 60% = SAR 40, which is far less than the specialty coffee market accepts. Its advantage is simplicity and assured coverage of variable cost. Its drawback is that it ignores what the customer is willing to pay and what competitors charge, so you may sell below your real value, or above what the market accepts. 2. Competitor-based pricing You look at the prices of alternatives, then set yours close to them, higher if you offer more value, or lower if your positioning is economical. Its advantage is realism; its drawback is that it may make you copy others without knowing whether their prices are profitable at all. 3. Value-based pricing You base the price on the value the customer feels, not on your cost. A gift box with three types of coffee, a brewing tool and a card explaining each origin may sell for SAR 150 even though it costs SAR 60, because what the customer buys is "a special gift worthy of the person receiving it," not just coffee. This method needs a deep understanding of the customer, which interviews reveal. 4. Penetration pricing You start with a temporarily low price to win customers quickly, then raise it gradually. It is risky if not calculated well: customers who came for the cheap price may leave when it rises, and you may lose money on every sale until then. The most common beginner's mistake is pricing too low for fear that nobody will buy. The result is a venture crowded with orders that loses money. Test different prices on real customers before deciding; you may be surprised to find that the higher price did not reduce demand.

search.c: Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Finance and Funding | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 9-7 Profit Is Not Cash: Cash Flow
search.t: A venture can be profitable on its income statement and still be unable to pay the rent. The reason is that accounting profit differs from cash flow , the actual movement of money into and out of the account at a given time. Example: Hamsa received a large order from a company for 300 gift bags for its employees, worth SAR 16,500, with the company paying two months after delivery. On paper this is excellent profit. But the venture needs to buy the beans and bags now (SAR 7,500) and pay this month's rent and salary (SAR 9,000). If there is not enough in the account, the venture may stumble while being "profitable." To avoid this: Keep a cash reserve covering several months of fixed costs, especially at the start. Ask for a down payment on large orders. Negotiate payment terms with suppliers. Track cash flow monthly: How much will come in, and when? How much will go out, and when? Separate the venture's account from your personal account from day one; mixing the two means you never know whether the venture is making or losing money.

search.c: Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Finance and Funding | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Every venture needs money to start or to grow. Funding sources differ in their terms and cost, and in what they ask of you in return. The first question before looking for funding: Do I really need it now? Many ventures can start small with their own resources, prove their model, and then seek funding on better terms. search.c: Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Finance and Funding | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: When a startup relies on investors, funding usually comes in successive rounds, each tied to a stage of the venture's maturity: Pre-seed : an idea and a prototype, with funding usually from the founders, family and grants. Seed : the product exists and has early customers, with funding from angel investors and early-stage funds. Series A and beyond : the business model has proven itself, the goal is expansion, and funding comes from venture capital funds. When someone invests in your venture in exchange for a stake, they implicitly set a value on the venture. If you offer an investor 10% of your venture for SAR 100,000, you are saying the venture is worth SAR 1 million after the investment (100,000 ÷ 10%), and 900,000 before it. You must justify this value with numbers and evidence. With each new round new investors come in, and the founders' share of ownership falls; this is called dilution . Dilution is not necessarily bad: owning 40% of a company worth ten million is better than owning 100% of a company worth a hundred thousand. But you must understand it before you sign.

search.c: Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Finance and Funding | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Costs are classified as start-up, fixed and variable, and each plays a different role in the calculation. Contribution margin is what each unit contributes to covering fixed costs, and the break-even point = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin. The contribution margin is the same for every extra unit, while the average profit per unit and the profit margin rise with sales. Start-up costs are recovered from profits after passing the break-even point. Profit is not cash; negative cash flow can bring down a profitable venture. Every funding source has its advantages and cost, and investment for a stake means diluting the founders' ownership.

search.c: Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Finance and Funding | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Start-up costs Costs paid once when the venture begins. Contribution margin Selling price minus the variable cost per unit. Net profit What remains of revenue after deducting all costs and statutory obligations. Profit margin Net profit ÷ revenue; it rises with sales because fixed costs are spread over more units. Break-even point The sales volume with neither profit nor loss. Cash flow The money actually coming in and going out over a period. Dilution The fall in the founders' ownership share as new investors join.

search.t: 10 Chapter 10 Legal and Ethical Aspects An idea may be strong and the market promising, and then the venture stumbles because of a dispute between partners, a trade name registered to someone else, or a regulatory violation. In this chapter we introduce the legal options for starting a venture in Saudi Arabia, the importance of an agreement between founders, the types of intellectual property, personal data protection, and the ethics that preserve a venture's reputation. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, you should be able to: Identify the common legal forms for starting a venture in Saudi Arabia. Explain the basic types of intellectual property. Commit to business ethics and the protection of customer data.

search.c: Chapter 10: Legal and Ethical Aspects | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 10-1 Why Should an Entrepreneur Care About Legal Matters?
search.t: People with new ideas tend to postpone legal matters: "Let's start first and sort out the paperwork later." During small-scale testing this may be acceptable within limits. But ignoring these matters for long can cost a venture dearly: a trade name you built your reputation on turns out to be registered to someone else, a dispute between partners has nothing to govern it, a fine arrives because the activity needed a license you never obtained, or customer data leaks. This chapter does not aim to make you a legal expert, but to help you know the right questions to ask, and the bodies to turn to. Regulations and procedures in Saudi Arabia are updated constantly, and the information here is general and simplified for educational purposes. Always check the official website of the competent authority before taking any step, and consult a specialist on contracts and important decisions.

search.c: Chapter 10: Legal and Ethical Aspects | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 10-2 Legal Forms for Starting a Venture
search.t: Entrepreneurs choose the legal form of their venture according to the nature of its activity, the number of partners, the level of risk, and their plans for growth and investment. You do not need to start with the largest form; many ventures start in a simple form and move to a larger one as they grow. 1. Freelancing Suits those who offer services based on individual skill, such as design, programming, translation, training, photography, writing and consulting. It is practiced formally through the freelance document issued by the freelance platform of the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development. It is one of the easiest ways to test a service idea without setting up a business, and allows a student or employee to start a side activity within the rules. 2. Home-based business Activities practiced from home, such as cooking, handicrafts and tailoring, have dedicated licenses and programs that allow legal selling under rules related to the type of activity and product safety, and some bodies offer support and financing programs for them. 3. Sole proprietorship A business owned by one person, registered with a commercial registration. Its key feature is that the owner and the business are one legal person : the owner is liable for the business's debts and obligations from their personal assets. It is simple to set up and run, and suits small ventures with limited risk. 4. Limited liability company The most common form for small and medium ventures with more than one owner (it can also be set up by one person). Its main advantage is that a partner's liability is limited to their share of the capital: if the company stumbles, claims do not extend to their personal assets, except in cases the law specifies. It therefore protects partners more than a sole proprietorship does. 5. Simplified joint stock company A new form introduced by the Companies Law that came into effect in Saudi Arabia at the start of 2023. It was designed to suit startups and entrepreneurs, because it allows more flexibility in organizing shares and in investors entering and exiting, compared with traditional forms. Form Suits Liability Freelancing Individual professional services Personal Sole proprietorship A small commercial activity with one owner Personal, extending to the owner's assets Limited liability company Small and medium ventures with partners Limited to the partner's share Simplified joint stock company Startups expecting investors to join Limited Registration and licenses Commercial registrations are issued and companies are formed through the Ministry of Commerce and the Saudi Business Center platform, which brings many procedures together in one place. Depending on the activity, you may need additional licenses: a municipal license for shops, or approvals from the authorities responsible for food and drugs, health, tourism or education. So always ask: Which authority regulates this activity?

search.c: Chapter 10: Legal and Ethical Aspects | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Noam Wasserman's research at Harvard, collected in The Founder's Dilemmas , shows that many startups stumble because of problems between the founders themselves, not because of the market. Partnerships often start with enthusiasm and trust between friends, who feel that writing an agreement is "awkward" or a sign of "distrust." Then disputes appear when the venture grows or stumbles: Who owns how much? Who decides? Why does one of us work more than the other? So write a founders' agreement from the start: a document that clearly answers questions such as: Shares : how much does each partner own, and on what basis (money, time, experience, the idea)? Roles and responsibilities : who handles what? Who makes the final decision in each area? Commitment : how much time will each partner give? When will each go full-time? Resolving disagreements : how do we settle a dispute? By majority, or through a third-party arbitrator? A partner's exit : what happens to their share if they decide to leave or do not commit? How is it valued? Profits : how are they distributed, and when? How much is reinvested? Some companies use vesting , under which a partner earns their share gradually over years of work, so if they leave early they take only what they have earned. This protects the venture from a partner who takes a large stake and then stops working.

search.c: Chapter 10: Legal and Ethical Aspects | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Intellectual property is the set of rights the law protects for the products of the mind and creativity. It is among the most important assets of a modern venture: your brand, your design or your software may be worth more than all your equipment. The competent body in Saudi Arabia is the Saudi Authority for Intellectual Property . Its main types are: 1. Trademark The name, logo or symbol that distinguishes your products or services from others. Registering it gives you the right to stop others from using a similar mark in the same field. One of the most important tips: search before you choose the name . Make sure it is not registered to someone else, then register it early, before you spend on identity and marketing. 2. Patent Protects an invention that is new (not previously disclosed), involves an inventive step (not obvious to experts in the field), and is industrially applicable . It gives its owner an exclusive right for a set period. Registration takes time and money, and it is sought only for genuine technical inventions. 3. Copyright Protects creative works: texts, images, designs, music, software and digital content. The right arises as soon as the work is created, and it can be documented and registered to support proof of ownership. 4. Industrial design Protects the distinctive external appearance of a product (its shape, lines and colors), not its function. For example, the shape of a bottle or the design of a piece of furniture. 5. Trade secrets Confidential information that gives the venture a competitive advantage, such as a recipe, a production method or a customer list. These are not registered, but protected through confidentiality and non-disclosure agreements with employees and partners. Can an idea be protected? A question that comes up often. The answer: an abstract idea cannot be protected . You cannot stop others from thinking of "an app for booking sports fields." What is protected is the specific execution: the name, the design, the software, the technical invention. So fear of your idea being stolen should not stop you from discussing it with customers and mentors; the value of an idea lies in its execution, and execution is hard to copy.

search.c: Chapter 10: Legal and Ethical Aspects | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Almost every venture collects data about its customers: names, mobile numbers, addresses, preferences. Saudi Arabia has issued a Personal Data Protection Law , overseen by the Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA). Its most important principles include: Collect only what you need : do not ask for data you will not use. Consent and clarity : tell the customer what you collect and why, and obtain their consent. Specific purpose : do not use data for anything other than the purpose you collected it for, and do not sell or share it without a legal basis. Protection : store data securely, and restrict who can access it. Data subject rights : the customer has the right to know what you hold about them, and to request its correction or deletion. Even in a small venture: if you collect subscribers' numbers in a group, you are responsible for ensuring they are not used for any other purpose.

search.c: Chapter 10: Legal and Ethical Aspects | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Ethics in entrepreneurship is not a luxury or excessive idealism, but a practical necessity: reputation is a small venture's capital, built slowly and destroyed quickly, especially in a close-knit society where experiences pass from person to person. The most important principles include: Honesty with customers : no exaggerated promises, no hidden flaws or fees, no fake reviews. Integrity with partners and investors : real numbers, even when they are weak. An investor who discovers you inflated your numbers will never trust you again. Respect for others' rights : do not copy a design, content or image without permission, and do not use someone else's trademark. Fairness to workers : wages paid on time, clear contracts and a respectful work environment. Responsibility toward society and the environment : a venture is part of its community and answers for its impact on it. Keeping commitments : honoring deadlines and contracts with suppliers and customers.

search.c: Chapter 10: Legal and Ethical Aspects | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: You can start with simple forms such as freelancing, then move to a sole proprietorship or company as the venture grows. A written founders' agreement protects both the venture and the relationship from disputes. Intellectual property protects the trademark, invention, content, design and trade secrets, not the abstract idea. Collecting customer data is a legal and ethical responsibility. Honesty, integrity and fairness are the foundation of a venture's reputation.

search.t: 11 Chapter 11 Pitching and Persuasion The pitch is the moment when weeks of work meet an audience that decides: will it care or not? A good pitch is a skill with a structure and rules that can be learned. In this chapter we cover the types of pitch, its persuasive structure, slide design, delivery skills and preparing for questions. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, you should be able to: Build a pitch with a clear, persuasive structure. Apply the rules of slide design and delivery. Prepare for questions and handle them.

search.c: Chapter 11: Pitching and Persuasion | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 11-1 What Is a Pitch, and What Is It For?
search.t: A pitch is a short talk in which a venture owner presents their idea to a specific audience, with the aim of persuading them to take a next step. The audience may be a judging panel in a competition, an investor, a potential partner, a supporting organization, or even a major customer. A common mistake is for the idea's owner to think the goal of the pitch is to explain everything , so they stuff it with details, numbers and features, and the listener comes away exhausted, remembering nothing. In fact a pitch has one goal : for the listener to become interested and want a next step, such as a second meeting, a trial, support or investment. The details come in the questions and in later documents. So before designing your pitch, answer two questions: Who is my audience? An academic panel cares about method and evidence, an investor about market size and return, a customer about the benefit to them, and a supporting organization about social impact. The same pitch is delivered with a different emphasis for each audience. What exactly do I want from them? If you do not know what you are asking for, the listener will not know how to help you.

search.c: Chapter 11: Pitching and Persuasion | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: 1. The elevator pitch Its name comes from the idea that you meet an important person in an elevator and have the length of the ride, 30 to 60 seconds, to spark their interest. It answers only four questions: Who are you? What is the problem? What is your solution? And why does it matter? It is useful everywhere: at events, and whenever someone asks "What do you do?" Example: "Many older people need a companion for their medical appointments, and their children have to take time off work. We provide trained companions from health-sciences graduates, with simple booking and a price lower than a day's leave. We trialed the service with twelve families in Hail, and nine of them booked it again." 2. The short pitch Three to five minutes, common in competitions, hackathons and course presentations. It covers the whole basic structure briefly. 3. The full pitch Ten to twenty minutes, delivered in meetings with investors and supporting organizations, with more detail on the market, the financial model and the growth plan.

search.c: Chapter 11: Pitching and Persuasion | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 11-3 The Structure of a Persuasive Pitch
search.t: Most successful pitches follow a similar structure, because it answers the questions in the listener's mind in their natural order. Here is what each part should contain: 1. The opening The first 15 seconds decide whether the listener will pay attention. Start with a short story about a real person you met, a question that makes the audience think about their own experience, or a surprising, reliable number. Avoid the conventional opening: "Hello, we are team so-and-so, and our idea is…" 2. The problem Make the listener feel the problem before presenting the solution. Who suffers from it? When? What does it cost them? Use the words of the people you interviewed; a real quote from a customer is more powerful than any description you write yourself. 3. The solution What do you offer, and how does it solve the problem? Explain it simply, and preferably show it: a picture, a prototype or a short clip. Do not drown in technical features; focus on what changes in the customer's life. 4. The market Who are your customers, and roughly how many are there? Use the realistic bottom-up estimate explained in Chapter 5. 5. The business model How do you make money? Who pays, and how much? A sentence or two is enough. 6. Traction (the evidence) This part is what separates a strong pitch from a weak one. What has actually happened? How many people did you interview? What did you learn? How many tried the prototype? How many signed up, ordered or paid? Actions are stronger than expectations, and a small real number is stronger than a large imagined one. 7. Competition and advantage What are the alternatives, and why are you different? Do not say "There is no competitor"; the panel will take it as a sign of weak research. 8. The numbers Price, cost, contribution margin, break-even point, and the funding you need, if any. A few clear numbers are better than a full financial table nobody reads. 9. The team Who are you, and why are you the best people to carry out this idea? Link the team's skills and fields to what the venture needs. 10. The ask (call to action) End with a clear and specific request: "We are looking for an organization to host the trial for a semester," or "We need SAR 30,000 for 10% to run the service in three neighborhoods." A pitch that ends without an ask leaves the listener not knowing what to do.

search.c: Chapter 11: Pitching and Persuasion | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Guy Kawasaki, the well-known entrepreneur and investor, proposed in The Art of the Start a rule he called 10/20/30 : ten slides, twenty minutes, and a font size of at least 30 points. The rule's purpose is to force you to be brief and focused. In a short pitch (3–5 minutes), cut back further. Practical principles include: One idea per slide : a slide carrying five ideas conveys none of them. Pictures and numbers instead of paragraphs : a photo of a real customer, or one big number, says more than a list of bullet points. Little text : the audience cannot read and listen at the same time. If you write everything you will say, they will read it and stop listening to you. Do not read from the slide : the slide supports what you say; it does not replace it. Clear contrast and readable type : make sure the slides can be read from the back of the room. The last slide : carries the ask and your contact details, because it stays on screen during questions.

search.c: Chapter 11: Pitching and Persuasion | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Story People remember stories far more than numbers and abstract arguments. Chip and Dan Heath explain in Made to Stick that messages that stay in memory are simple, unexpected, concrete, credible, emotional, and told as stories. So start with the story of a real person you met, and come back to them at the end. Simplicity Test your pitch on someone outside your field. If they do not understand it, it is too complicated. Avoid technical terms unless the audience is specialized. Confidence and presence A clear voice at a moderate pace, eyes on the audience rather than the screen or paper, a steady stance, and natural hand movement. Confidence does not mean claiming to know everything, but believing in what you present and knowing its limits. Practice A pitch that looks spontaneous has been rehearsed many times. Practice aloud, with a timer, at least three times, preferably in front of people who will give you frank feedback. And record yourself on your phone once; you will discover habits you had not noticed. Teamwork in the pitch If the team presents together, divide the parts in advance so each member presents what they do best, and agree on smooth linking sentences for handing over between speakers. Nobody interrupts anyone, and not everyone talks about everything.

search.c: Chapter 11: Pitching and Persuasion | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: The outcome of a pitch is often decided in the questions rather than the pitch itself, because they reveal how well the team understands its venture. So prepare by writing a list of the hard questions you expect and practicing your answers. They include: Who is your real competitor, and why would the customer choose you? How do you know people will pay? What if someone with greater resources copies you? How did you arrive at this number? What is the biggest risk facing the venture? Why are you the right team? When you answer: listen to the whole question, answer briefly and directly, and do not slip into a tense defense. If you do not know the answer, say so honestly, and say how you will find out: "We haven't tested this yet; our plan is to test it by…" That answer builds far more trust than an invented one the panel can expose with a single follow-up question.

search.c: Chapter 11: Pitching and Persuasion | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: The aim of a pitch is for the listener to want a next step, not to know everything. A persuasive structure starts with the problem, moves through the solution, market, model and evidence, and ends with a clear ask. Slides support the speaker rather than replace them: one idea, a picture or number, and little text. Story, simplicity and practice are the keys to delivery, and honesty is the best answer to a question you cannot answer.

search.t: 12 Chapter 12 Growth and Lessons from Success and Failure In this chapter we close the book by looking beyond the beginning: how ventures grow, why many of them stumble, and what we learn from stories of success and failure. The aim is not to memorize the stories, but to draw out patterns that help you make better decisions in your venture and your work. Chapter objectives After studying this chapter, you should be able to: Explain the main causes of startup failure. Distinguish between growth and scaling. Draw practical lessons from stories of success and failure.

search.c: Chapter 12: Growth and Lessons from Success and Failure | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: A large share of new ventures stumble in their first years. This fact should not frighten you, but make you ask: What are the recurring causes, and how can I avoid them? Many reports and studies have analyzed why ventures stumble, among them the work Tom Eisenmann, professor of entrepreneurship at Harvard, gathered in Why Startups Fail , and similar causes recur in them. We explain them here: 1. No real market need One of the most frequent causes in these studies. The team built a technically good product, but not enough people need it, or do not need it enough to pay. This usually happens because the team fell in love with its idea and did not test it with customers before building. 2. Running out of money The venture spent its money before reaching sufficient revenue. The cause may be underestimated costs, premature expansion, or a cash flow problem despite profits on paper. 3. The wrong team Missing core skills (a team of technical people with no one who sells, or the reverse), disputes between partners, or weak commitment. 4. Competition Ignoring or underestimating competitors, or the arrival of a stronger competitor with greater resources against which the venture had no protective advantage. 5. Pricing and cost The contribution margin is too small, or the break-even point is too far from realistic sales, so the venture cannot survive however hard it tries. A common form is a venture that delights the customer but exhausts whoever delivers it: it consumes their time or money beyond what the customer pays, so workers leave or the entrepreneur burns out and exits the market. This is what we explained in "A Deal Where Every Party Wins" in Chapter 6. 6. A weak product, or ignoring customers A product that does not deliver on its promise, or a poor experience, combined with a refusal to listen to feedback and adjust. 7. Timing Entering too early, before the market or technology is ready, or too late, after the market has settled on strong competitors. Notice that most of these causes can be discovered early and cheaply with what you have learned in this book: customer interviews reveal the absence of need, honest calculation reveals a weak margin, and small experiments reveal a weak product before you spend much.

search.t: Once a venture proves that its model works, a new stage begins: growth. Specialists distinguish between two concepts that may look similar: Growth : increasing revenue with a roughly similar increase in resources and costs. Example: a restaurant opens a second branch; revenue roughly doubles, but so do rent, staff and equipment. Scaling : increasing revenue much faster than costs. Example: a digital learning platform adds a thousand new subscribers at very little extra cost, because the same content is delivered to everyone. The question that reveals your venture's scalability: Does each new customer require a large new cost? Services based on human time (consulting, one-to-one training) are hard to scale, because the hours in a day are limited. Ventures based on a product that can be replicated (software, digital content, platforms) scale more easily. This does not mean non-scalable ventures are bad; it means they grow in a different way. Ways to grow Igor Ansoff identified four basic growth strategies, known as the "Ansoff Matrix": Existing products New products Existing markets Market penetration : selling more to current customers and attracting similar ones (lowest risk) Product development : new products for your current customers New markets Market development : the same product in a new city or segment Diversification : a new product for a new market (highest risk) Other routes to growth include franchising , granting others the right to operate your model and brand elsewhere in exchange for fees and a percentage, so your venture grows with others' money and effort while you maintain the standards; and partnerships with organizations that reach customers you cannot reach. Beware of reckless growth Expanding before the model has proven itself in the first market, or with money out of proportion to revenue, is one of the greatest dangers facing successful ventures. A second branch opened before the first is profitable can bring both down. The rule: master it, then expand.

search.t: Here are documented, well-known stories, not to memorize them, but to draw out recurring patterns: Kodak: current success can blind you to coming change Kodak owned digital photography technology early: one of its engineers built a prototype digital camera in 1975. But the film business was very profitable, so the company hesitated to push a technology that could compete with its main product. As digital photography and then smartphones spread, its business declined until it filed for bankruptcy in 2012. The lesson: do not let your current success stop you from seeing change; if you do not disrupt your own product, someone else will. Nokia: size does not protect against slow response Nokia led the world mobile phone market for many years. With the arrival of smartphones with touchscreens, new operating systems and app stores, it was slow to change, its share fell very quickly, and it sold its phone division in 2014. The lesson: size and reputation are not enough; the ability to adapt quickly is what protects a venture. Instagram: watch what customers actually do It began as a feature-packed app for checking in at places. Its founders noticed that people used only the photo feature, so they removed everything else and focused on it. The lesson: customers' real behavior is more truthful than your plans, and simplifying can be the greatest innovation. Amazon: start narrow and master it, then expand Amazon began in 1994 as an online store for books only, because books are easy to ship, and so varied that no single shop can stock them all. After mastering this market, it gradually expanded into other categories. The lesson: focusing on a narrow market at the start gives you the chance to master it before expanding. HungerStation: an ordinary daily need, and a model that satisfies its parties It started in Saudi Arabia in 2012 to solve a problem everyone knew: to order food you collected paper menus from restaurants and phoned them, only to find the line busy or the order misunderstood. It brought the restaurants together on one platform, with ordering at the press of a button and courier tracking. The global company Delivery Hero acquired a majority stake in 2016, and the remaining shares in 2023. The lesson: it invented neither the food nor the restaurants; it changed the way people order, by building a model in which the customer, the restaurant, the courier and the platform all gain, as we saw in the faces map in Chapter 6. Tamara: understanding the local market is an advantage Founded in 2020 to offer "buy now, pay later" in interest-free installments, in a form that respects Islamic principles. It solved the customer's cash-flow problem at the moment of purchase and increased the merchant's sales. At the end of 2023 it raised a funding round of about $340 million that took its valuation past $1 billion. The lesson: a well-known global model can succeed locally when it is adapted to people's culture and values, which is what we called "compatibility" in Chapter 4. WeWork: fast growth is no substitute for a profitable model It offered shared workspaces to companies and individuals, grew very fast and attracted huge investment, expanding into many cities around the world on long leases. But its costs were far higher than its revenue, its public offering faltered in 2019, and it filed for bankruptcy protection in 2023. The lesson: this is the "reckless growth" we warned about: expanding before the model has proven its profitability magnifies the loss rather than fixing it. Student projects that stop There is also a local pattern that anyone who has taught this course knows: student projects that start with great enthusiasm in a competition or course, then stop after a few weeks. The recurring causes: no strong need, relying on enthusiasm without a plan, lack of time, and the team scattering after the course ends. The lesson: continuing takes more than a nice idea; it takes evidence of need, commitment and a realistic plan.

search.s: 12-4 How Do You Deal With Failure?
search.t: Failure is a natural part of entrepreneurship. The question is not whether you will fail, but how you will deal with failure when it happens: Separate yourself from the venture : the failure of an idea does not mean you are a failure. It means a hypothesis was wrong. Ask: What did we learn? Write down the lessons as soon as the experiment ends, before you forget them: What did we expect? What happened? Why? What will we do differently? Fail early and cheaply : this is the purpose of every testing tool in this book. Failing in a week with SAR 500 is a lesson; failing after a year with all your savings is a disaster. Know when to stop : persistence is a virtue, but ignoring repeated evidence is not persistence; it is stubbornness. Decide in advance what would make you stop or pivot. Learn from others' failures : read the stories of ventures that stumbled and ask their founders; they are the cheapest lessons you can get.

Most important of all, take one small step this week.

search.c: Short Classroom Activities | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: 30 circles 5 minutes Breaking the fear of “strange” ideas · Materials: A sheet with 30 empty circles Turn as many circles as possible into different things (a clock, a ball, a face…) within 3 minutes. Compare your count with a classmate’s: who went beyond the familiar? Who combined more than one circle? Ask: why did we stop at the first ideas? Fluency comes before quality, and breaking rules nobody set. The worst possible idea 5 minutes Generating ideas without pressure · Materials: Nothing Pose a problem (such as long waits at clinics). Each team proposes the worst possible solution within two minutes. Reverse the bad solutions: what does each one become if we flip it? Reverse brainstorming frees up thinking, and many good ideas come out of the worst ones. Sell me this pen 5 minutes The difference between features and benefits · Materials: A pen or anything on the table A volunteer tries to sell the pen to the instructor within a minute. The class notices: did they talk about the pen or about the buyer’s need? The second attempt starts by asking the buyer about their need. The customer doesn’t buy a product; they buy a solution to their need. The value of an ordinary thing 7 minutes Seeing opportunity in the familiar · Materials: A paper clip or an empty water bottle Each team takes a very ordinary object. Within 4 minutes: what is the best way to create value from it for someone? The most valuable idea (not the strangest) wins. Value doesn’t live in the object, but in the need it meets. Today’s problem 5 minutes Training the observing eye · Materials: A phone At the start of the lecture, each student writes one problem they noticed on their way to the university. The instructor reads 5 of them at random. The class votes: which one does more than half the room experience? Opportunities are all around us, but we need to train our eyes to see them. The 3-minute interview 10 minutes Listening instead of persuading · Materials: Nothing Each student interviews a classmate they don’t know about “the last time you were late for something important.” No suggesting solutions. Just ask: What happened? Why? What did you do? Swap roles, then share the strangest reason you heard. A good interview reveals what people don’t say in questionnaires. What does it really cost? 10 minutes A feel for numbers · Materials: A picture of a familiar product (a cup of coffee, a meal, a car wash) Each team estimates the product’s variable ingredient costs. Then estimates the shop’s fixed monthly costs. They calculate in the calculator: how many cups must the shop sell each day to break even? Profit isn’t just the selling price minus the materials; fixed costs eat a lot. The tweet 5 minutes Clarity of the idea · Materials: A phone Write your venture idea in a post of no more than 20 words. Pass it to another team: did they understand who the customer is and what the benefit is? Rewrite it based on what they didn’t understand. If your idea can’t be understood in one line, it won’t be understood in a pitch. Pivot or persevere? 10 minutes Making a decision based on evidence · Materials: A scenario card the instructor reads out Read a short scenario: “A team trialed a car wash service in company parking lots. Only 3 people ordered, but 20 asked: do you clean and sanitize the inside of the car?” Each team decides within 3 minutes: do we persevere, adjust, or change direction? Why? Discuss: what evidence did you rely on? Changing direction based on evidence isn’t failure; it’s intelligence. Is everyone smiling? 10 minutes Thinking about all the parties in a venture · Materials: Paper and pen The instructor presents a common idea (a mobile barber, a mobile workshop, a mobile car wash). Each team draws a face for each party: the customer, the service provider and the venture owner, and roughly calculates how many customers are served a day and what price works.
