search.t: Appendix 2 Guide to Developing the Venture Idea Students develop their idea throughout the semester in nine parts, as a mini business plan, and then submit their final version. Each part sets out what is required, an example from a single venture, “Baroda,” an air-conditioner maintenance subscription, and a common mistake to avoid. The parts can be filled in, saved and downloaded on the interactive course page .

search.c: Guide to Developing the Venture Idea | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: What is the problem or gap? Who has it, and when? Convince the reader of three things: that the problem exists, that you understand it, and that there is a real need to solve it. Cite what you heard in your interviews (how many, and phrases people said) and any reliable number. Write in this part: One clear sentence defining the problem: Who has it? When? What is its effect on them? The evidence: how many people did you interview? What did they say? (Quote a phrase or two in their own words.) How do people deal with the problem now, and why isn’t that enough? Example: “Air conditioners in many homes break down at the peak of summer, so families wait two or three days for a technician in intense heat, and sometimes pay large sums to repair faults that simple maintenance could have prevented. We interviewed eight families; six said at least one unit broke down last summer, and one mother said: ’I called three technicians. One didn’t answer, the second said in two days, and the third came and asked for an amount I couldn’t tell was fair or not.’” Avoid: describing the problem in general terms such as “people suffer from the heat,” relying on your personal opinion without any interviews, or writing the solution instead of the problem.

search.c: Guide to Developing the Venture Idea | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Describe your customer precisely: “families in new neighborhoods with four or more AC units” is clearer than “people.” Roughly how many are there? How do they deal with the problem now? Write in this part: A precise description of the customer: age or life stage, place and behavior. An approximate number of potential customers, and where this number came from. Who pays? (This may differ from the beneficiary, like a father who pays for a service his son benefits from.) Example: “Families living in villas or large apartments in residential neighborhoods, with four or more AC units, where the head of the household usually pays. After them we target small shop owners. We estimated the number of homes in three nearby neighborhoods at about (…) from a field count, and we expect about 10% of them to be interested in the service, based on our interviews.” Avoid: writing “everyone” or “all the city’s residents,” or citing large numbers with no source.

search.c: Guide to Developing the Venture Idea | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.s: 3 The solution and what sets it apart
search.t: What is the product or service? What sets it apart from the alternatives (price, speed, quality, ease, proximity)? Make sure the solution works for you as its provider, for the customer, and for the other parties (supplier, courier, partner). Write in this part: What exactly is the solution? How does the customer get it, step by step? What sets it apart from current alternatives? One clear advantage is better than five general ones. Is the solution profitable for every party: you, the customer, and the supplier, courier or partner? Is the amount the customer will pay enough for everyone to earn? (Fill in the stakeholder balance below this part.) Your message in one sentence (use the message maker in the tools). Example: “An annual subscription with two scheduled maintenance visits (before summer and in mid-summer), priority for breakdowns within 24 hours, and a photo report after every visit. The advantage: a known, fixed price and a guaranteed appointment instead of searching for a technician when something breaks. And because we schedule visits by neighborhood, the technician visits several nearby homes on the same day, so he earns a good income, the price stays reasonable for the family, and we keep a worthwhile margin.” Avoid: describing the solution in general terms such as “a smart app that solves every household problem,” adding many features unrelated to the problem you heard, or a solution that delights the customer but is exhausting or loss-making for whoever delivers it.

search.c: Guide to Developing the Venture Idea | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Is it something people buy daily, or once a year? Roughly how large is demand? Who offers a similar solution, and what indirect alternatives do people use? Don’t write “there is no competitor”; there is always an alternative. Write in this part: Is the product bought daily, weekly or on occasions? Direct competitors (offering the same solution), indirect competitors, and alternatives (what people do now). A simple comparison table: you versus two or three competitors on price, quality and ease. Example: “Demand is seasonal and recurs every year. Competitors: independent technicians (sometimes cheaper, but their appointments are not guaranteed and their prices are unclear), large maintenance companies (reliable, but more expensive and focused on businesses), and the most common alternative: waiting until the unit breaks down and then looking for a technician.” Avoid: writing “there is no competitor,” which means you didn’t search, or that there is no need.

search.c: Guide to Developing the Venture Idea | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: What is the simplest version you tested (a sketch, a page, an order form, a manual trial)? With how many people? What changed in your idea after the test? Changing direction based on evidence counts for you, not against you. Write in this part: What is the simplest version of the solution you tested? (A sketch, a post, an order form, delivering the service by hand to a few people.) How many people did you test it with? And what actually happened? What did you learn? What did you change in your idea after the test? Example: “We posted a simple ad in two neighborhood groups with a booking link for a maintenance visit at a trial price. 19 families booked within two weeks, and we carried out the visits with a cooperating technician. 11 of them asked about an annual subscription, and we discovered that families care about the photo report more than we expected, because it reassures them the work was really done, so we made it a core part of the service.” Avoid: settling for “we’ll test later,” or showing the idea only to your friends and asking whether they like it. And remember that changing the idea after testing counts for you, not against you.

search.c: Guide to Developing the Venture Idea | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: We focus on monthly operations. Write the fixed costs item by item, then the variable cost per unit and the selling price; the result is calculated automatically. Ask yourself about the expected sales: are they reasonable? Write in this part: Fixed monthly costs item by item (rent, salaries, subscriptions, utilities). The variable cost per unit (materials, packaging, delivery), and the selling price. Expected monthly sales, and where this expectation came from. The break-even point is calculated automatically; comment on it: is it realistic? Example: “The price of a visit in the subscription is SAR 150, and its variable cost SAR 60 (materials 35, fuel 15, messages and payment fees 10), so the contribution margin is SAR 90. Fixed costs are SAR 9,000 a month (a technician’s salary, a vehicle lease and the scheduling system subscription), so we need 100 visits a month to break even, about 4 visits a day, which is feasible if the visits are close together. Equipping (SAR 12,000) is a start-up cost that we did not include in the monthly calculation.” Avoid: including start-up costs (equipment and fit-out) in the monthly costs, forgetting small costs such as packaging and delivery, or assuming large sales without evidence.

search.c: Guide to Developing the Venture Idea | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: How many people does the venture need? Who does what? Are the workers on monthly salaries or contracted per job? And what happens to the team as you expand? Write in this part: Who is on the team, and who handles what? Whom do you need to add to actually run the venture? (On salary, or contracted per job.) What changes in the team if the venture grows? Example: “Three members: the first for operations and scheduling visits, the second for marketing and customer contact, and the third for accounts and purchasing. We need one salaried technician at the start, and we add technicians contracted per visit at the peak of summer.” Avoid: listing team names without roles, or ignoring who will actually work in the venture.

search.c: Guide to Developing the Venture Idea | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: How do you reach your customer? What is your message in one sentence (use the message maker)? And how do you keep them so they come back and buy again? Choose one or two channels where you know your customer is. Write in this part: Your message in one sentence. One or two channels where you know your customer is, and why you chose them. An offer that gets the customer to try it the first time. How do you get the customer to come back and recommend you? Example: “Our message: (A cool summer with no breakdowns, and a guaranteed technician appointment.) We reach customers through neighborhood groups and real estate offices, with a free inspection for the first 20 subscribers, and a free extra month for anyone who brings in a neighbor who subscribes, because neighboring subscribers bring our visits closer together and save the technician’s time.” Avoid: listing every platform without focus, or simply saying “we’ll market on social media.”

search.c: Guide to Developing the Venture Idea | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: Is expansion costly? Does each new branch or city need start-up costs and staff? And what is the first small step you would take if you decided to actually start? A venture that does not grow usually withers. Write in this part: Is expansion costly? (Does each new location or city need premises, staff and equipment?) Where could the venture expand: new customers, new places, or complementary products? What is the first small, realistic step if you decided to actually start next month? Example: “After three neighborhoods, we expand to others with new technicians, each covering a defined area. We can add small shops and residential compound subscriptions. First step: run the service for one summer in two neighborhoods and reach 60 subscribers.” Avoid: large expansion plans unconnected to what you have achieved, such as “we’ll cover every city in the Kingdom in the first year.”

search.c: Guide to Developing the Venture Idea | Entrepreneurship 101 | Dr. Omar A. Alsamani
search.t: We conducted at least 5 interviews with people who have the problem, not all of them our friends. The problem is written precisely (who? when? how much?), not in general terms. We named at least one alternative or competitor. We distinguished between start-up, fixed and variable costs. We tested a simple prototype with real people. The writing is in our own voice; if we used AI, it was as an assistant in developing and building ideas, not for the final writing. ✦ ✦ ✦
